Moreover, the cost of products includes personnel expenses, distribution costs, and profit margins; an increase in the CGPI therefore does not directly correspond to an increase in the CPI. However, now that firms are increasingly passing on cost increases to selling prices, higher corporate goods prices need to be regarded as pushing up consumer prices more than in the past, and attention should be paid to the recent 7 percent increase in the CGPI.

The SPPI includes not only services such as dining-out and accommodation, which fall outside the realm of manufacturing, but also distribution- and information-related costs. This index is therefore driven largely by personnel expenses.
Personnel Expenses

While the macroeconomic indicators I just mentioned are indeed important in assessing prices, having worked for many years in a commercial business, I am particularly interested in understanding in detail how things work and what mechanisms lie behind them. Let me start by examining personnel expenses.

The left panel of Chart 3 indicates the data for wages excluding overtime pay and bonuses, which closely approximate base pay. Recent data show a growth rate of around 3 percent. The wage increase of 5-6 percent mentioned in the annual spring labor-management wage negotiations in Japan includes seniority-related wage increases. In terms of how individuals feel in their daily lives, that is probably the more relevant figure. However, because a firm's workforce is constantly turning over, with older workers retiring and new graduates being hired, wage data that more closely reflect base pay should be examined.

The wage growth rate is a key determinant of monetary policy. Economic activity can be stable only when there is a moderate cycle of firms passing on higher wages to selling prices and then responding to the ensuing inflation with wage increases. A situation where neither wages nor prices rise, as seen during Japan's deflationary period, and a situation where both rise excessively, as in the first oil shock, are both unfavorable for the economy.

As shown in the right panel of Chart 3, the rate of change in real wages -- which is calculated by subtracting the inflation rate from the rate of change in nominal wages -- is what matters for households. Even if wages increase, household income will be negative on a net basis unless the wage hikes keep up with inflation. However, the year-on-year rate of change in real wages has finally turned positive in Japan. If the inflation rate moderates to around the Bank's target level of 2 percent while wage hikes of around 3 percent continue, the rate of change in real wages will remain positive. That said, attention needs to be paid to the fact that the recent inflation rate has been suppressed by subsidies and other government policy factors. Corporate managers generally raise wages in line with the inflation rate and pass on these increased wages to selling prices; even a temporary decline in the inflation rate could therefore affect wage negotiations.

I often hear that the combination of wage increases and policy interest rate hikes is causing difficulties for firms. It is indeed not hard to imagine the significant challenges business owners are facing, given labor shortages and the need to comply with the increase in the minimum wage in Japan. However, if the inflation rate cannot be contained at an appropriate level, this could lead to a vicious cycle in which firms have to further raise wages to retain workers. The Bank considers that, to ensure that the wage increases firms have managed to achieve are not in vain, it is important to manage the inflation rate through appropriate monetary policy and thereby maintain real wage growth.

Regarding recent labor shortages in Japan, let me explain one set of data that has caught my attention. The left panel of Chart 4 shows labor-related data. The number of employed persons has increased due to the growing participation of women and seniors in the labor force, while working hours have decreased due to working-style reforms and other factors. Labor input, calculated by multiplying the number of employed persons and working hours, has remained more or less flat, albeit on a slight decline. To be sure, there are mismatches among industries and job types -- industries such as construction and nursing care services are facing severe labor shortages. Hence, if some areas are facing shortages while overall labor input has remained flat, that implies that some areas are not experiencing shortages. I am paying attention to how wage increases in the latter areas will take shape.

The right panel of Chart 4 presents the distribution of the growth rate in the number of employed persons by prefecture, and shows that regional disparities are widening. Given that the growth rate in the number of employed persons for Fukui Prefecture is roughly 10 percent below the national average, I believe the business leaders participating in the meeting today might be feeling an acute sense of labor shortage.
Distribution Costs

Next, I would like to touch on distribution costs. The left panel of Chart 5 shows the year-on-year rate of increase in motor freight transportation costs -- a component of the above-mentioned SPPI -- which surged to almost 6 percent for July. The rate remains high, even though gasoline prices have declined on a year-on-year basis, as suggested in the right panel of Chart 5, due to the reintroduction in mid-March 2026 of gasoline subsidies; this could imply a substantive pass-through of personnel expenses triggered by high crude oil prices.

Since higher distribution costs are passed on to a wide range of prices, they could affect underlying inflation, which I will discuss later. Of course, distribution costs and personnel expenses are not the only components of production costs, so a rise in these costs does not directly translate into an increase in the inflation rate.
Food Prices
Let us now look at food prices, which have a large weight in the CPI.

The left panel of Chart 6 illustrates the breakdown of the CPI over the past few years, which I mentioned earlier. Specifically, the bar graph shows, in descending order, the contribution to the year-on-year rate of change in the overall CPI of the prices of (1) services such as communications, hotel services, and education; (2) goods excluding food and energy; (3) rice-related items, which consist of both rice itself and processed food that uses rice as an ingredient, such as box lunches, rice balls, and rice crackers; and (4) other food excluding fresh food, shown in dark blue.

As you can see, food prices have a significant impact on CPI inflation. To make this clearer, the right panel of Chart 6 plots the year-on-year rates of change in the prices of some of the components in the left panel. Fresh food and energy, for which prices fluctuate significantly, are often excluded when examining prices. The price surge in rice-related items is pronounced, reflecting an unprecedented rise in rice prices, which doubled from 2024 to 2025. Comparing the other three components, however, while the year-on-year rates of change in the prices of services and goods have both been stable in the range of 1-2 percent, the rate of change in the price of processed food that does not use rice as an ingredient has been high, in tandem with the rise in rice prices. The subsequent start of a decline in rice prices was expected to present challenges to food manufacturers, since they had been raising selling prices along with the rise in rice prices. Nevertheless, factors such as higher distribution costs and the increase in the prices of packaging materials and food trays could create an environment that would prompt another round of price increases, sparking concerns about a reacceleration of food price hikes. While the prices of rice and crude oil have garnered attention, I consider that, from a long-term perspective, the price of food in general is a key determinant of future inflation.
Other Risk Factors
In addition to the Iran situation, the Bank is closely monitoring developments in foreign exchange rates and in AI-related demand as risk factors to prices.

Foreign exchange policy falls under the jurisdiction of the government, and the Bank does not set its policy interest rate to respond directly to changes in foreign exchange rates. That said, the impact of the yen's depreciation on prices has become more pronounced than in the past and warrants close attention.

Mounting AI-related demand is pushing up prices not only of semiconductors themselves, but also of semiconductor production equipment, copper, and power-generation facilities. The effects of this demand increase are also being felt in general consumer goods, including personal computers and household electrical appliances. The rapid global expansion in AI-related demand can be regarded as a demand shock that exerts strong upward pressure on prices as well as on corporate profits and other economic variables. Unlike high crude oil prices or the yen's depreciation, however, it is not simply the case that it would be better if AI-related demand subsided -- such demand is also a factor that mitigates the negative effects of high crude oil prices and supports the global economy. If momentum in AI-related demand stalls, therefore, the impact on Japan's economy would be significant. Moreover, unlike the United States and China, Japan is not a global provider of AI services; rather, the country is benefiting from the demand generated by AI development, particularly for semiconductor-related materials and equipment. It is necessary to bear in mind, therefore, that these benefits could diminish once the expansion of AI production capacity comes to a halt.
II. Economic Indicators
Real Interest Rate

Next, I would like to explain some representative indicators the Bank is monitoring. Having already touched upon prices, exchange rates, and wages, let me start with the two types of interest rates that are referred to in relation to the Bank's monetary policy.

The real interest rate is calculated by subtracting the inflation rate from the nominal interest rate. Chart 7 shows 1-year and 10-year real interest rates. These rates are obtained by subtracting inflation expectations -- calculated using a synthesis of multiple statistical data -- from the current yields on Japanese government bonds (JGBs). Until last year, both of these rates were significantly negative. Now, however, they are at around 0 percent, reflecting factors such as the Bank's policy interest rate hikes and the rise in long-term interest rates.

That said, the 1-year to around 2-year real interest rates are still negative. As a result, increases in the value of real estate purchased through borrowings exceed the interest paid on the loans, and this could consequently set off a surge in real estate prices. In addition, firms might hasten their investment more than is necessary, while household savings might lose their real value. I therefore believe the negative real interest rate situation should be addressed as soon as possible, since Japan's economy is no longer in deflation.
Neutral Interest Rate
Although the neutral interest rate is an indicator that central banks always keep in mind in conducting monetary policy, this rate cannot be expressed as a specific figure.

The calculation of the neutral interest rate begins with estimating the natural rate of interest, which neither heats nor cools economic activity. As shown in the left panel of Chart 8, the natural rate of interest is estimated using various theoretical models, and the estimates fall within a fairly wide range. These are the latest figures, released in March this year. At the time they came out, it had been two and a half years since the previous release. The overall range has remained largely unchanged, and is estimated to be between minus 0.9 percent and plus 0.5 percent.

The natural rate of interest is the real interest rate before adjusting for inflation. Adding 2 percent, which is the Bank's price stability target, makes this rate nominal, somewhere in the range of 1.1 to 2.5 percent. This estimated range is what the media refers to as the neutral interest rate. For comparison, the policy interest rate currently set by the Bank is 1.0 percent.

Given that various methods are used to estimate the neutral interest rate and that it can only be indicated within a fairly wide range, this rate is simply a reference. In particular, since policy interest rate hikes over the past two years have brought the rate close to the estimated range of the neutral interest rate, the Bank will need to more thoroughly examine factors such as prices, employment, and financial conditions in considering further rate hikes.

Unlike in Europe and the United States, the policy interest rate in Japan is lower than the estimated range of the neutral interest rate, as shown in the right panel of Chart 8. Until recently, many other central banks around the world continued to cut policy interest rates to bring them closer to the neutral interest rate, while the Bank of Japan has been raising its rate. The reason Japan alone has a policy rate that is below the estimated range of the neutral interest rate could be attributable to differences in the degree of impact from global inflation following the COVID-19 pandemic and in the responses to this inflation. As shown in Chart 9, post-pandemic inflation was not as high in Japan as it was in Europe and the United States. Japan was thus able to maintain a negative interest rate policy. There is also a view that Japan's mild inflation was attributable to the inability of firms to easily pass on higher raw material costs to selling prices because of prolonged deflation in this country.

In dealing with U.S. tariffs, while sharing the same concerns about economic deterioration, Japan and other countries took opposite policy approaches -- raising or cutting the policy interest rate. Currently, the Iran situation has led countries around the world to tilt toward a stance of rate hikes to address inflationary concerns, and central banks in many countries are actually raising their policy interest rates. That said, financial conditions in Japan remain accommodative. If inflation accelerates here, there is a risk that the Bank might inevitably need to implement a rapid policy interest rate hike. To complete the normalization of monetary policy in Japan, I am convinced that the Bank needs to raise the policy interest rate further, so that it falls solidly within the estimated range of the neutral interest rate, thereby ensuring the flexibility needed to swiftly adjust the policy rate in either direction, depending on economic conditions.
Impact of Policy Interest Rate Hikes on Firms and Households
It is also important to monitor the impact of policy interest rate hikes on firms and households.

Chart 10 shows corporate demand for funds. There is no indication that the recent policy interest rate hikes have dampened firms' appetite for funding -- on the contrary, their appetite appears to have increased. However, there are concerns about potential overheating in corporate investment activities. Investing requires both discernment and prudence. Failed investments could rapidly cool corporate activities and hinder Japan's economic growth.

To observe the direct impact of policy interest rate hikes on households, let us look at the total amount of households' balance sheets in Japan and the asset and liability structure by age group in Chart 11. This indicates that, overall, households are in a net asset surplus when comparing cash and deposits with loans. However, younger generations face the burden of housing loans, although recent wage increases for this age group have been relatively higher than for other age groups.
Underlying Inflation

Let me also discuss underlying inflation, which the Bank uses as a reference. Underlying inflation excludes fresh food prices, which fluctuate significantly, and temporary factors -- namely, the surge in rice prices, the crude oil shock, and the effects of government measures such as tax hikes and subsidies. It is an important concept in conducting monetary policy, which, in Japan, currently aims at achieving sustained inflation of 2 percent.

As with the natural rate of interest, underlying inflation cannot be expressed as a specific figure. The Bank's quarterly Outlook for Economic Activity and Prices (Outlook Report) had previously shown selected indicators for underlying inflation. From the April 2026 Outlook Report, the Bank has started to show more of the indicators that it monitors on a regular basis in this regard, such as those using statistical methods and economic models. Charts 12 and 13 summarize these indicators.

As you can see, developments in the indicators vary, and the impression they give may differ depending on the viewer. That said, my impression is that, although the underlying inflation rate remains below 2 percent, it is very close to the 2 percent target.
III. Recent Monetary Policy
Policy Interest Rate
Lastly, I would like to discuss the Bank's monetary policy, focusing in particular on its policy interest rate and balance sheet.

As shown in Chart 14, the Bank has made an exit from the prolonged period of unprecedented monetary easing and has implemented five policy interest rate hikes since March 2024. Before each Monetary Policy Meeting (MPM), which is held eight times a year, the Bank's Policy Board members thoroughly examine a wide range of data, such as on business fixed investment and financial market conditions, in addition to the data I explained earlier.

While the Bank will continue to raise the policy interest rate and adjust the degree of monetary accommodation in response to developments in economic activity and prices as well as financial conditions, what is most vital from now on is to ensure that the underlying inflation rate does not significantly exceed 2 percent.

The rising prices of fuel and chemicals due to the Iran situation may turn out to be a temporary shock, but also have the potential to further push up costs that would have far-reaching effects, such as distribution costs. This applies to food as well: in addition to higher domestic distribution costs, the rise in maritime shipping fees for imported raw materials and in the price of imported fertilizers are some factors that contribute to food price hikes. There are concerns that the price hikes in these goods may not be temporary shocks but rather represent more enduring trends that risk pushing up overall prices.

Given that the underlying inflation rate is very close to 2 percent, as I explained earlier, and that financial conditions have been accommodative, the Bank will continue to raise the policy interest rate and adjust the degree of monetary accommodation. It will consider the timing and pace of adjustment, while examining the likelihood of realizing the baseline scenario and the risks to the outlook presented in the July 2026 Outlook Report, including the impact on economic activity and price developments from crude oil prices, AI-related demand, and developments in foreign exchange rates.
Balance Sheet

Following its decision at the September 2025 MPM on a guideline for the disposal of exchange-traded funds (ETFs), the Bank decided at the June 2026 MPM to halt the reduction of its purchase amount of JGBs. The expression "to halt the reduction" may sound a little confusing, but it simply means that the Bank will keep its amount of JGB purchases constant for the time being, from fiscal 2027. After having conducted large-scale JGB purchases during the period of unprecedented monetary easing, the Bank has been gradually reducing the amount of its purchases since summer 2024, but has now arrived at the decision to halt the reduction. The Bank's annual JGB purchases amounted to as much as 135 trillion yen at their peak four years ago but, from fiscal 2027, the level will be about 2 trillion yen per month, or roughly 24 trillion yen annually.

Since JGBs carry maturities, the amount outstanding will decrease simply by dint of the Bank reducing the amount of its purchases. As shown in the right panel of Chart 15, the Bank's JGB holdings stood at nearly 590 trillion yen at their peak. This accounted for about 50 percent of the amount outstanding of JGBs issued, which was remarkably high relative to the proportion of government bonds held by central banks in other major economies. Looking ahead, however, the Bank's JGB holdings are expected to decline steadily.

What JGB maturities the Bank should hold in the future is likely to become a topic of growing importance. Since assets are matched against liabilities, and the Bank's principal liabilities are current account deposits held by financial institutions at the Bank and banknotes, determining the appropriate way to match assets and liabilities is an issue that involves some complexities and will be examined.

This does not necessarily mean that the overall balance sheet ought to be reduced to levels prior to the Bank's implementation of unprecedented monetary easing. In the wake of the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, it is possible that demand for central bank reserves has been changing, mainly due to the tightening of international liquidity regulations and the strengthening of risk management by financial institutions. Taking this possibility into account, the Bank will ascertain what the appropriate size of its balance sheet is.
Thank you.

Monetary Policy Statement, 2026-27 Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee October 5 to 7, 2026

Monetary Policy Decisions The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) held its 63rd meeting from October 5 to 7, 2026, under the chairmanship of Shri Sanjay Malhotra, Governor, Reserve Bank of India. The MPC members Dr. Nagesh Kumar, Shri Saugata Bhattacharya, Prof. Ram Singh, Dr. Poonam Gupta and Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya attended the meeting. 2. After a detailed assessment of the evolving macroeconomic and financial developments and the outlook, the MPC voted unanimously to increase the policy repo rate under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) by 25 bps to 5.50 per cent. Consequently, the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate stands adjusted at 5.25 per cent and the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate and the Bank Rate at 5.75 per cent. The MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening. Growth and Inflation Outlook Global Outlook 3. Since the last MPC meeting in August 2026, the re-escalation of the conflict in West Asia and the consequent sharp volatility in crude oil prices has kept the global economy in a state of flux. Global growth has remained resilient. Acceleration of inflation in key economies has prompted a shift towards hawkish monetary policy. The US Fed hiked by 25 bps in September. The Fed commentary thereafter along with rate tightening by major systemically important central banks have reinforced expectations of higher global policy rates. Tighter global financial market conditions coupled with fiscal sustainability concerns in major economies are keeping global bond yields at record high levels. With a resolution of the West Asia conflict remaining elusive, significant downside risks to the global outlook remain, including further tightening of global financial conditions, continuing elevated AI-related asset valuations and high public debt. Domestic Outlook 4. Notwithstanding these persisting global headwinds, the Indian economy has remained resilient. As per National Statistics Office (NSO) estimates, real GDP growth in Q1:2026-27 at 7.8 per cent was higher than expected. Strong private consumption and fixed investment, rebound in merchandise exports and sustained buoyancy in services exports supported growth. On the supply side, the manufacturing sector grew at a robust pace. Services sector activity strengthened further, owing to buoyant domestic and external demand. 5. In Q2, available high frequency indicators for July-August suggest sustained momentum in domestic economic activity. Domestic demand remains resilient and is well supported by robust external demand with merchandise exports registering double-digit growth. 6. Looking ahead, global economic uncertainty will continue to have some bearing on domestic economic activity. While energy prices and supply chain pressures have continued, their near-term trajectory remains uncertain amidst the lingering West Asia conflict. Their adverse impact is being contained with active diversification of supply sources. Deficient south-west monsoon and strong El Niño conditions pose risks to agriculture sector’s outlook and rural demand, although healthy buffer of foodgrains and proactive policy interventions by the government are expected to mitigate the impact. Furthermore, continuing momentum in services and broadly stable employment conditions are likely to support urban demand. Strong capacity utilisation, robust credit flows and the government’s thrust on infrastructure are expected to sustain investment activity. While services exports are expected to remain buoyant, bilateral trade agreements should boost merchandise exports. 7. Taking all these factors into consideration, real GDP growth for 2026-27 is projected at 7.1 per cent, with Q2 at 7.2 per cent; Q3 at 6.9 per cent and Q4 at 6.8 per cent. Real GDP growth for Q1:2027-28 is projected at 7.1 per cent. The risks are evenly balanced ( Chart 1 ). 8. CPI inflation increased to 4.8 per cent in August 2026 from 4.5 per cent in July. While the increase has been predominantly on account of higher inflation in food and fuel groups, core inflation has also picked up indicating some signs of widening price pressures. Food price increases have become more broad based along with notable spikes in certain items such as sugar and onion. The uptick in fuel inflation in August largely reflected unfavourable base effects. Core inflation increased to 4.2 per cent and core inflation, excluding precious metals, increased to 2.9 per cent in August. The weighted share of items in headline CPI recording inflation above 4 per cent increased steadily to about 37 per cent in August. 9. The near-term outlook on inflation points towards continued pressures from supply side on account of the deficient monsoon, ongoing El Niño conditions and high energy and other commodity prices, the pass through of which is still continuing. Considering all factors, CPI inflation is projected to be 5.2 per cent for 2026-27 with Q2 at 4.9 per cent; Q3 at 6.0 per cent; and Q4 at 5.7 per cent ( Chart 2 ). Inflation for Q1:2027-28 is projected at 5.6 per cent with risks being evenly balanced. Core inflation is projected at 4.4 per cent for 2026-27. Rationale for Monetary Policy Decisions 10. The MPC noted that the global context on account of geopolitical developments remains challenging. Nonetheless, the Indian economy has been strong. The economic momentum remains broad-based. The economy is expected to remain resilient. 11. In the light of available data, it is clear that inflation and its outlook are not benign as they were last year with headline CPI inflation expected to average almost 5.8 per cent in the next three quarters and core inflation projected at 4.4 per cent this year. In this milieu, recalibrating the policy rate is imperative. 12. As regards supply side inflation, monetary policy primarily acts by curtailing second round effects (inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, etc.), which take time to manifest and are difficult to extract from available data. Apart from data related to inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, indicators of generalisation of inflation like core inflation and diffusion indices are used for this purpose. It may, however, be kept in mind that it is difficult to distinguish between the second-round effects and the indirect impact of supply side pressures (in production cost through energy and other inputs) as both are present in these indicators. While there is some evidence of elevated inflation expectations and generalisation of inflation, there are only limited signs of supply side pressures getting embedded in pricing behaviour. 13. Similarly, while there is limited evidence of demand side pressures, risks in view of strong growth in monetary and credit aggregates exist. 14. Considering all these factors, the MPC unanimously voted to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent. The MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening. It only signals that given the current conditions, rate cuts are off the table in the near term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on the evolving conditions and the outlook. The duration and extent of rate hike cycle would be contingent on the actual growth-inflation developments and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, the extent of broadening of price pressures and second round effects of the supply shock, as also the impact of demand impulses. 15. Two members - Dr. Nagesh Kumar and Prof. Ram Singh - were of the view that the stance be retained at neutral. 16. The MPC remains committed to its price stability mandate and will endeavour to progressively align inflation with its target. 17. The minutes of the MPC’s meeting will be published on October 21, 2026. 18. The next meeting of the MPC is scheduled for December 2 to 4, 2026. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1264

Renewed energy-price pressures stoked inflation pressures and prompted a more hawkish stance from leading central bank. Fiscal sustainability concerns, persistent inflation, and geopolitical uncertainty raised bond yields, while equity markets remained volatile amid lingering concern on valuations technology stocks. Amidst global uncertainty, domestic financial markets underwent intermittent volatility during H1:2026-27. Transmission to lending and deposit rates plateaued with status quo in policy rate during H1:2026-27. Bank credit growth became broad based and strengthened further. The domestic economy showed resilience in H1:2026-27, despite continued global uncertainty amidst the conflict. The supply-side pressures were alleviated by proactive policy measures by the government that ensured adequate supply of key inputs. Real GDP recorded a growth of 7.8 per cent in Q1:2026-27 reflecting strong momentum in underlying economic activity. Aggregate demand remained strong on the back of both private consumption and investment. Net external demand was also robust and contributed significantly to growth. On the supply side, both manufacturing and services sectors recorded strong growth in Q1. High frequency indicators suggest continued buoyancy in domestic economic activity, albeit with some moderation compared to Q1. Stable employment conditions, congenial financial conditions, revival in corporate investment, and a pickup in goods exports – nurtured by bilateral FTAs and diversification – are expected to support economic activity going forward. Sustenance of private consumption growth will be essential for broad-based recovery in private capex. Headline CPI inflation increased sequentially, rising above the target during June-August, driven by a sustained positive price momentum. Food and fuel groups led to this increase, reflecting adverse weather conditions and the sharp rise in energy prices following the West Asia conflict. Core inflation registered a pick-up with some signs of generalisation in recent months. Input cost pressures have accentuated, but the pass-through has remained limited so far. Going forward, India’s macroeconomic outlook remains resilient supported by domestic demand and strengthening investment, despite persistent global uncertainties. The outlook remains vulnerable to geopolitical developments, volatility in global energy markets and weather-related uncertainties. Weak monsoons coupled with strong El Niño, protracted geopolitical tensions, rising international commodity prices, additional frictions in global trade and tightening of global financial conditions could adversely impact the growth outlook. Persistent supply-side pressures in food and volatile global energy prices pose risks to the domestic inflation outlook, particularly through second-round effects amid strong growth impulses. The interplay of these factors will shape the evolving growth–inflation dynamics, with the balance of risks depending on developments in global growth, crude oil prices, exchange-rate movements, and domestic food supplies. I. External Environment Global growth remains resilient, mainly supported by AI-related investment and fiscal measures, but faces renewed supply-side shocks from the West Asia conflict, elevated oil prices and trade related frictions. Inflation has accelerated again, prompting central banks to shift towards a more cautious and hawkish monetary policy stance. Financial markets remain volatile amid higher yields, geopolitical tensions and shifting risk sentiment. Global growth has remained resilient despite facing persistent headwinds from supply shocks. However, the near-term growth forecasts have been revised downwards by several multilateral agencies, as key supply chains remain disrupted and crude oil prices remain elevated. Investment in artificial intelligence (AI) and related technologies, along with increased international trade in AI-related hardware, has supported global economic activity. Fiscal support across countries has sustained economic activity but also heightened concerns about rising public debt and reduced fiscal buffers. Along with higher inflation and higher-for-longer monetary policy expectations, these concerns have contributed to a sharp rise in government bond yields across major jurisdictions. Inflation, which had been moderating towards the end of 2025, began to accelerate following the supply shock triggered by the West Asia conflict. Crude oil prices rose to levels not seen in recent years. At the same time, other commodity prices also increased, feeding into higher goods inflation even as services inflation remained elevated in several major economies. Consequently, central banks that had been moving towards monetary policy normalisation last year adopted a more hawkish stance following the onset of the conflict. Several advanced and emerging market economies (EMEs) have tightened monetary policy or maintained a cautious stance, while only a handful have reduced policy rates to support growth. Of late, the US Fed and the European Central Bank (ECB) have been placing greater emphasis on incoming data and their monetary policy frameworks in decision making, rather than on forward guidance. The Fed’s hawkish stance, combined with elevated crude oil prices, contributed to risk-off sentiment and portfolio outflows from EMEs, exerting depreciation pressure on their currencies. Sovereign bond yields have hardened globally, particularly in advanced economies (AEs), on concerns over rising public debt, debt-servicing costs and persistent inflation concerns. Emerging market equities experienced selloffs during Q3 of 2026, with some recovery in August while advanced economy equities gained, driven by technology stocks and healthy corporate profits. The US dollar gained, as higher bond yields, expectations of a hawkish Fed, and safe-haven demand amid geopolitical uncertainty outweighed intermittent weakness. I.1 Global Economic Conditions In 2026 so far, global growth has remained resilient, even as near-term growth forecasts have been revised downwards amid the fragile geopolitical situation in West Asia. The growth outlook is dependent on the de-escalation of the conflict, as key supply chains continue to face disruptions, and oil prices remain elevated. In its July 2026 World Economic Outlook update, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) lowered its global growth projection for 2026 by 10 bps to 3.0 per cent, reflecting the uncertainty around the outlook. However, it raised its projection by 20 bps for 2027 to 3.4 per cent, as the impact of the conflict remains less than what was anticipated earlier, while AI-related investment and productivity gains are likely to fuel growth. Meanwhile, the OECD, in its September 2026 Interim Economic Outlook, marginally raised its global growth forecast by 10 bps to 2.9 per cent for 2026, while lowering its 2027 projection by 10 bps to 3.0 per cent. While AI-related activity is expected to provide continued support, stronger price pressures and elevated interest rates are likely to weigh on near-term growth momentum. Among AEs, real GDP growth in the US remained resilient in 2026, supported by robust consumer spending and investment, including continued private investment in AI and related technologies. Growth, however, moderated in the second quarter, reflecting a downturn in government spending, slower investment and export growth, while stronger consumer spending partly offset these effects ( Table I.1 ). Since April 2026, labour market conditions have softened, with non-farm payroll growth slowing down during summer and weakening further in September, while the unemployment rate remained largely stable. The composite PMI continued to expand strongly in August, recording a 52-month high, driven by services while manufacturing remained healthy amid improved business optimism and new orders. Consumer sentiment, as measured by the University of Michigan Survey, declined in September to its lowest level in four months, amid growing concerns about elevated prices. Overall, underlying economic activity in the US remains resilient. Among other AEs, growth in Japan in 2026 so far has been largely driven by the external sector. GDP growth strengthened in Q1, with net exports making the largest contribution. Growth moderated in Q2 due to slowdown in domestic demand, particularly private investment, though this moderation was offset largely by a strong contribution from net exports. The composite PMI continued to expand in August, driven by manufacturing while services also improved. On the other hand, GDP growth recovered in the euro area in Q2 after stagnating in Q1, primarily driven by strong growth in Ireland and Spain. Household and government expenditure continued to provide support to economic activity. The composite PMI expanded in August at the same pace for the second consecutive month as the moderation in services was offset by solid expansion in manufacturing amid growth in new orders and factory output. In the UK, GDP growth rebounded in Q1 2026, supported by services and broad-based expansion across the economy, with gross capital formation and household consumption driving growth on the expenditure side. Growth moderated in Q2, reflecting weaker household consumption and lower inventory accumulation amid the adverse effects of the conflict in West Asia. Among high-frequency indicators, the composite PMI expanded in August for the second consecutive month, driven by services sector activity offsetting the moderation in manufacturing. Among major EMEs, China’s growth is facing challenges from subdued consumption and a weaker external sector in 2026, with GDP growth moderating in Q2 from Q1. The composition of growth has also undergone a shift, with the share of net exports in GDP growth declining significantly relative to 2025, while the share of gross capital formation increased. Investment growth remains uneven, with stronger activity concentrated in AI-related and high-tech sectors. High-frequency indicators also point to subdued activity, with composite PMI slowing in July as both manufacturing and services sector activity moderated. In August, however, PMI rebounded as output and new orders increased in both the sectors but remained below the average for 2026. Brazil’s GDP growth remained stable at 1.8 per cent (y-o-y) in Q1, marking the third consecutive quarter of growth at this pace. The agriculture and services sectors supported growth while industrial activity declined. In Q2, however, GDP expanded by 2.0 per cent, driven by recovery in industrial sector and sustained growth in agriculture. Industrial sector benefited from higher oil and gas extraction amid higher energy prices. Brazil’s composite PMI remained very close to the neutral line in the last few months, reflecting weakness in the economy as new orders continue to fall. Russia’s economy contracted in Q1, reflecting weak manufacturing and construction activity, although services remained resilient. Activity recovered in Q2, led by manufacturing, while agriculture remained subdued. The composite PMI also returned to expansion in August, ending five consecutive months of contraction, supported by stronger output and new orders. In South Africa, GDP growth accelerated in Q1, driven by a recovery in agriculture, increased mining activity, and stronger momentum in services, before moderating in Q2 led by a contraction in manufacturing and mining. Composite PMI continued to remain around neutral line in August amidst subdued new orders and weak business confidence. The Asian Development Bank (ADB), in its September 2026 outlook, projected ASEAN 1 growth at 4.7 per cent in both 2026 and 2027. The outlook remains subject to downside risks from the West Asia conflict, elevated energy and commodity prices, weaker external demand and heightened global uncertainty. Turning to high-frequency indicators, the OECD’s composite leading indicators (CLIs) showed that most economies remained above their long-term trend in Q2 and Q3 (till August) of 2026 ( Chart I.1a ). The global composite PMI expanded at its quickest pace in August in more than two years, with broad-based expansion in both output and new orders ( Chart I.1b ). The services sector continued to expand in August for the fifth straight month, while the manufacturing sector remained solid. World merchandise trade expanded for eleven consecutive quarters through Q2:2026, with growth remaining robust and exceeding expectations. Both EMEs and AEs contributed to the expansion, though the impulse came largely from EMEs, with moderation in contribution by the AEs as frontloading of US imports moderated. In July 2026, world merchandise trade volume growth remained strong at 6.0 per cent (y-o-y), with EMEs contributing 3.2 percentage points and AEs 2.8 percentage points ( Chart I.2a ). The surge in trade of electronic components related to AI offset the negative impact of the conflict in West Asia. The WTO, in its March 2026 update, revised its projection for global merchandise trade volume growth from 0.5 per cent to 1.9 per cent in 2026, reflecting strong AI-related trade and a smaller-than-anticipated impact of tariffs. The Goods Trade Barometer (September 2026, WTO) remained above trend at 102.0, with the electronic components and other goods linked to investment in artificial intelligence (AI) indices indicating continued momentum in merchandise trade. Meanwhile, shipping costs remained elevated, with the Freightos Baltic Global Index staying higher in 2026 - above its 2025 average - reflecting the rerouting of vessels away from disrupted shipping corridors/chokepoints and continued capacity pressures ( Chart I.2b ). I.2 Commodity Prices and Inflation Commodity prices, as captured by the Bloomberg Commodity Index, have exhibited divergent movements, largely attributable to sector-specific fundamentals ( Chart I.3a ). Agricultural commodity prices have risen due to conflict-related disruptions to energy, fertiliser and shipping markets, adverse weather conditions and tighter crop-supply prospects. Global food prices, as reflected in the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) food price index, have increased since April 2026, mainly due to vegetable oils, cereals, and sugar ( Chart I.3b ). Gold prices declined through Q2 2026 amid expectations of higher interest rates. Gold prices gained overall in Q3 as heightened geopolitical uncertainty, including renewed tensions in West Asia, boosted safe-haven demand. Periods of weakness in the US dollar and lower expectations of further tightening by the Fed also supported prices, outweighing the drag from rising bond yields and the stronger dollar in September. Among base metals, copper and zinc prices have continued to rise, supported by tightening supply conditions. Aluminium prices rose to a four-year high in early June amid concerns over supply disruptions from the West Asia conflict, before moderating as the US dollar strengthened and Chinese exports increased ( Chart I.3c ). Energy prices surged in April, largely reflecting the sharp increase in Brent prices, before moderating as supply disruptions eased. However, the re-escalation of tensions in West Asia led to a renewed increase in energy prices in August and September, amid concerns over disruptions in regional oil production and shipping ( Chart I.4a ). Against this backdrop, developments in global oil supply buffers and demand conditions remain important. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) is currently placed at roughly 284 million barrels, at its lowest level since October 1982. Strategic releases and inventory drawdowns helped to cushion shocks. Also, weaker import demand by China due to release of stocks and domestic demand destruction helped offset some supply pressures. However, if the disruptions last longer, there is lower flexibility available to deal with supply shortages ( Chart I.4 b&c ). Consumer Price Inflation Inflationary pressures have re-emerged following a temporary moderation, driven primarily by renewed energy and commodity price pressures amid heightened West Asia tensions. The US personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation metric, saw inflation surge through May, driven by a sharp increase in gasoline prices before falling subsequently as energy prices stabilised. In the UK, headline inflation has been lower in Q2 2026, mainly due to easing food inflation, before edging up in Q3 so far on rising energy and housing prices. In the euro area, energy prices and persistently high service inflation drove the CPI inflation higher, except for a modest correction in June due to a reversal in crude prices. In Japan, inflation rose steadily from April, reflecting a slower decline in energy prices as subsidies were scaled back in Q2, alongside imported inflation from yen depreciation. Inflation rose further in Q3, on elevated food prices and transportation costs, despite lower electricity prices. In EMEs, inflation has been divergent, reflecting differences in domestic demand conditions and supply-side pressures across economies. In Brazil, the headline CPI rose due to food and beverages, then fell as food, transport, and housing prices moderated. Inflation in South Africa accelerated from April to June, driven predominantly by higher fuel and transport costs, before easing in July as fuel prices declined and food-price inflation moderated. In Russia, CPI inflation eased until May on easing food pressures before edging higher due to fuel and a weaker rouble. China’s CPI inflation has remained subdued, supported by persistent food-price deflation ( Chart I.5b ). I.3 Monetary Policy Stance Since April 2026, monetary policy actions have diverged across economies. However, major advanced economy central banks turned more hawkish in Q3 2026, as renewed West Asia tensions raised energy prices and intensified inflationary pressures. Among major AEs, the US Fed held the target range at 3.50–3.75 per cent through July. In September, amidst persistent inflationary pressures, robust economic activity and stable labour-market conditions, the Fed unanimously raised the target range by 25 basis points to 3.75–4.00 per cent. The Bank of England has maintained the policy rate unchanged at 3.75 per cent in the last six meetings, noting little evidence so far of material second-round effects from the energy shocks while reiterating that future policy decisions depend on how the energy shock evolves and its impact on inflation. The ECB raised its key policy rates by 25 basis points in June and again in September, taking the deposit facility rate to 2.50 per cent. The decisions reflected persistent energy-driven inflation pressures associated with the conflict; however, indirect and second-round effects have remained largely contained. The Bank of Japan (BoJ) continued policy normalisation, raising its policy rate by 25 basis points each in June and September to 1.25 per cent. The moves reflected persistent inflationary pressures, owing to higher import costs amid yen depreciation, with future policy decisions to be guided by developments in economic activity and prices. The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates in May amid elevated inflation and capacity pressures, and again in September as fuel-price pass-through and stronger-than-expected growth intensified inflation risks. The Bank of Canada maintained status quo as longer-term inflation expectations have remained anchored and there was little evidence that oil prices had fed through more broadly to goods and services prices. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand hiked the policy rate by 25 bps for the first time in three years in July and then again in September by the same magnitude to 2.75 per cent. The monetary policy committee considered gradual withdrawal of monetary stimulus as appropriate to steer inflation to the 2 per cent target, while supporting growth and employment ( Chart I.6a ). Among key EMEs, Brazil continued its monetary easing cycle, with the central bank reducing the Selic rate in successive meetings amid signs of moderating economic activity and easing inflationary pressures. The Bank of Russia has gradually reduced its key rate as economic growth edged lower. China has held its benchmark rate at 3.0 per cent for more than a year amid ample liquidity. South Africa raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 7.25 per cent in September, following a similar increase in May, amid rising inflation risks and concerns over potential second-round effects. The Bank of Thailand kept its policy rate unchanged, balancing weaker growth and subdued domestic demand against conflict-related, supply-driven inflation pressures. The Bank of Mexico cut its policy rate by 25 basis points to 6.5 per cent in May, marking the end of its easing cycle. In September, it kept rates unchanged but removed its earlier forward guidance, signalling greater policy flexibility ( Chart I.6b ). I.4 Financial Markets Global financial markets remained largely resilient yet volatile, guided by the interplay of AI-driven risk appetite, shifting monetary policy expectations, elevated sovereign borrowing needs, and persistent geopolitical tensions in West Asia. The stock-bond correlation in the AEs has shifted for the first time in decades, reflecting uncertainty due to supply-side shocks ( Box I.1 ). Box I.1: Stock–Bond Correlation in Advanced and Emerging Economies The equity–government bond return correlation is central to multi-asset portfolio diversification. Stock–bond return correlation is influenced by short-term rates, inflation, volatility, and economic growth (Aslanidis and Christiansen, 2012). Theoretical explanations link asset-price co-movement to macroeconomic conditions (Campbell et al., 2020), while changes in stock–bond correlation have important implications for portfolio diversification (Brixton et al., 2023). More recently, evidence from G7 economies suggests that the macroeconomic drivers of stock–bond correlation vary over time, with significant implications for portfolio risk and diversification (McMillan, 2026). After two decades of generally positive readings, the correlation in advanced economies turned sharply negative during the 2021–22 inflation surge and again in 2025 ( Chart I.1a ). Using a DCC-GARCH model, the analysis finds that stock–bond correlation in advanced economies follows an inflation-regime relationship. Inflation enters with a negative linear and positive quadratic term, implying that correlation is lowest near the inflation target and rises as inflation moves away from it ( Chart I.1b ). The implied turning point is 1.6 per cent, essentially at the 2 per cent target, and the real short rate is also positive and significant. The findings suggest that when inflation is moderate, government bonds tend to hedge equity-market risk. This mechanism, however, does not extend to emerging markets. Their correlation averages around +0.6 and never turns negative over the sample, while its relationship with domestic inflation is weak and statistically insignificant. A formal Wald test also rejects equality of the advanced- and emerging-market coefficients. Instead, global equity volatility (VIX) is the only significant explanatory variable. The results suggest that emerging-market government bonds behave more like risk assets than domestic safe havens, selling off alongside equities when global risk appetite deteriorates. Thus, their diversification benefits are not evident in the post-2008 sample, unlike in advanced economies. References: 1. Global equities advanced in Q2 2026, driven by continued momentum in artificial intelligence (AI) and related capital investment cycles ( Chart I.7a ). Geopolitical tensions in West Asia added sporadic volatility during the quarter. The announcement of a US–Iran ceasefire framework and a memorandum of understanding (MoU) eased concerns about a broader regional conflict. Energy prices recoiled, and investor sentiment improved as fears of a sustained disruption to global energy supplies diminished. During Q2, US equities advanced, supported by resilient corporate earnings and sustained investor enthusiasm for AI-related companies. In the euro area, equities posted solid gains, with IT outperforming amid strong corporate earnings and diversification by investors from US markets. In the UK, equity prices rose, although declines in energy stocks limited overall gains. Markets largely looked through domestic political developments, with investor sentiment remaining broadly resilient. Japanese equities delivered robust returns in Q2 as easing tensions in West Asia buoyed sentiment, while the yen – at a four-decade low against the US dollar – supported exporters. In Q3, major equity markets posted modest gains, although investor sentiment remained cautious amid expectations of further monetary tightening, elevated technology-sector valuations, and persisting tensions in West Asia. Equities gained in the US, supported by resilient corporate earnings and sustained AI optimism, with further support from the Fed’s commitment to combating inflation despite its hawkish stance. Euro-area equities declined in Q3 as higher energy prices and persistent inflation lifted bond yields and weighed on risk sentiment, while political uncertainty and fiscal concerns, added to investor caution. Japanese equities were affected by the global correction in AI-related stocks and also concerns surrounding a stronger yen which could weigh on exports. In the UK, equities made modest gains, supported by robust corporate earnings, and elevated commodity prices. Equity markets in most EMEs rose sharply in Q2:2026, outperforming global peers. Taiwan and Korea led market performance, driven by gains in memory and semiconductor stocks amid strong AI demand ( Chart I.7b ). In Q3, emerging-market equities surrendered the gains recorded in the previous quarter as the AI-led rally showed signs of fatigue. Renewed conflict in West Asia, heightened trade tensions, and expectations of a more hawkish Fed weighed on investor risk appetite. A global sell-off in government debt led by inflation persistence and high government deficits has raised borrowing costs. These pressures have been exacerbated by the West Asia conflict, which has driven up oil prices, leading investors to seek higher bond yields as the odds of rate cuts have largely diminished. Sovereign bond-market performance diverged in Q2: Japanese and US rates firmed up, while German and UK yields softened. Developments in West Asia continued to be a major driver of the market, with bond yields moving in tandem with oil prices. Yields on government bonds surged to multi-year highs around the middle of the quarter amid fears of further escalation but fell on signs of a possible US–Iran deal. In the US, rates were underpinned by a resilient labour market and elevated government debt, reinforcing expectations that monetary policy would remain tight. A combination of global inflation concerns, and domestic politics hit UK gilts. In April, the 10-year gilt yield hit its highest level since 2008, reflecting inflationary pressures from higher oil prices and concerns about budgetary and political vulnerabilities ahead of municipal elections. Higher oil costs and imported-inflation pressures from the yen supported expectations for BoJ policy hikes this year, while concerns about fiscal expansion contributed to upside pressure. In Q3, government bond yields in major AEs have risen amid persistent energy-price pressures and tighter monetary policy, while elevated public debt and renewed fiscal support have added to upward pressure on long-term yields. In the US, higher oil prices, persistent inflation concerns, and higher borrowing requirements pushed treasury yields higher. The Treasury’s decision in mid-August to expand buybacks of long-dated securities provided only temporary relief, as underlying inflation and term-premium pressures continued to weigh on the market. Elsewhere, government bond yields in the euro area, Japan and the UK moved up amid renewed inflation concerns from rising energy prices, while rate hikes and firm policy signals, along with country-specific fiscal risks and elevated sovereign borrowing requirements, added to the rise in yields ( Chart I.8 a ). Emerging-market 10-year sovereign bonds recorded a mixed performance, displaying divergent country-specific inflation, fiscal, and monetary policy dynamics. While favourable risk sentiment and easing expectations initially supported some markets, the subsequent rise in oil prices, US sovereign bond yields, and geopolitical tensions tightened external financing conditions, increasing borrowing costs and weighing more heavily on sovereigns vulnerable to fiscal and external risks ( Chart I.8b ). In currency markets, the US dollar strengthened in Q2 2026, supported by higher oil prices, heightened geopolitical tensions and still elevated inflation, which reinforced safe-haven demand and expectations of relatively tighter monetary policy. Most major currencies weakened against the US dollar, with the yen declining to a four-decade low despite large scale coordinated intervention by the US and the Bank of Japan. The euro also depreciated, while sterling demonstrated greater resilience. In Q3, the US dollar, which had remained broadly weak through much of the quarter, strengthened markedly in September. The rebound was driven by higher US bond yields and a repricing of expectations for further Fed tightening following the release of data suggesting resilient activity and persistent inflation concerns. Renewed geopolitical tensions in West Asia, elevated oil prices, and trade-related uncertainty also supported safe-haven demand for the dollar. Consequently, the dollar index rose by around 2.0 per cent during September to a near two-month high, although it ended Q3 only marginally higher. Against this backdrop, the renewed negative correlation between the S&P 500 and the US dollar since April indicates that the dollar has again provided a partial hedge during periods of equity-market stress, appreciating when risk sentiment deteriorated and weakening as risk appetite recovered ( Chart I.9 ). Shifts in monetary policy expectations, geopolitical developments, and global risk appetite can, however, quickly alter the stock–dollar correlation. The MSCI EM Currency Index rose driven by carry-seeking flows, supportive commodity prices and country-specific inflows. However, gains moderated late in the period amid renewed pressure from rising long-term US bond yields ( Chart I.10 a & b ). I.5 Conclusion The global economic outlook continues to be shaped by supply-side shocks emanating from the West Asia crisis, shifting trade tariffs, and the ongoing AI investment boom. Despite multilateral agencies projecting slower global growth in 2026, high-frequency indicators, including purchasing managers’ indices, point to resilient economic activity. Inflation has picked up in most economies, prompting central banks to adopt a more hawkish stance. Long-term bond yields have risen amid persistent inflation concerns, while equity markets have advanced, underpinned by the ongoing AI-driven investment boom. Introduction Global financial markets remained volatile amidst shifting expectations, persistent tensions in West Asia and rising fiscal concerns. Against this backdrop, domestic financial markets displayed intermittent volatility during H1:2026-27. System-wide liquidity surplus surged in September 2026 reflecting buoyant capital flows under the Reserve Bank’s swap facilities. Money market rates largely moved in line with the evolving liquidity conditions, with rates in Certificates of Deposit (CDs) and Commercial Papers (CPs) easing in Q2. The exchange rate exhibited two-way movements in H1. Monetary policy transmission to lending rate moderated during H1 amidst rate pause and funding pressure. Nonetheless, bank credit continued to grow robustly and financing from non-bank sources also increased. II.1 Liquidity Conditions and the Operating Procedure of Monetary Policy The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Act, 1934 requires the Reserve Bank to place the operating procedure relating to the implementation of monetary policy and changes thereto from time to time, if any, in the public domain. 1 During H1:2026-27, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) kept the policy rate unchanged in three successive meetings while retaining the neutral policy stance. Drivers and Management of Liquidity System liquidity, as measured by the net balances under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF), improved significantly in H1:2026–27 from a moderate surplus in H2:2025–26 ( Chart II.1 ). On a net basis, average daily absorption under the LAF increased to ₹3.21 lakh crore in H1:2026–27 from ₹1.43 lakh crore in H2:2025–26. Capital inflows and the build-up of government cash balances were the principal drivers of liquidity conditions in H1:2026–27. System liquidity remained in surplus during H1:2026-27 except for end-June when it briefly turned into deficit amidst tax related outflows. 2 In Q1, liquidity conditions improved initially supported by faster government spending, but it moderated thereafter due to increase in currency in circulation (CiC) and the RBI’s foreign exchange operations. Liquidity conditions improved in Q2, aided by capital inflows under the RBI's swap facilities ( Table II.1 ). With liquidity conditions remaining largely in surplus, banks’ recourse to the marginal standing facility (MSF) averaged ₹0.01 lakh crore during H1:2026-27, while average daily standing deposit facility (SDF) balances increased marginally 3 . The Reserve Bank remained nimble and agile in its liquidity management operations, ensuring sufficient liquidity in the banking system to support transmission to money market. With surge in liquidity surplus mainly due to FCNR(B) swaps 4 , the RBI conducted variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) operations of varying maturities, although several variable rate repo (VRR) operations were also undertaken mainly until July 2026 to tide over transient liquidity tightness and align overnight rates with the policy rate. Overall, the RBI conducted a total of 36 VRR and 51 VRRR auctions in H1. As on September 15, 2026, reserve money expanded by 8.5 per cent (y-o-y) as against 5.6 per cent a year ago. Adjusted for the first-round impact of CRR change, growth in reserve money stood at 11.9 per cent (9.4 per cent a year ago). II.2 Domestic Financial Markets Money market rates softened in H1:2026-27 in tandem with evolving liquidity conditions. G-sec yields eased until August before hardening in September, reflecting higher global yields, rising oil prices, and expectations of monetary tightening. Corporate bond yields moved in sync with G-sec yields, with a hardening bias, while risk premia showed mixed trends. Equity markets gained marginally despite heightened volatility in global financial markets and crude oil prices due to West Asia conflict. The foreign exchange market remained volatile amid shifting US policies and lingering conflict in West Asia. In the credit market, both bank and non-bank credit grew at a robust pace. II.2.1 Money Market During H1:2026-27, money market rates softened and remained mostly range bound amid large surplus liquidity conditioned by robust capital inflows, especially from FCNR(B) deposits under the Reserve Bank’s swap facility announced in June 2026. The weighted average call rate (WACR) – the operating target of monetary policy – generally remained within the policy rate corridor. However, with the significant rise in surplus liquidity, it moved downward towards the SDF rate, floor of the corridor, in September ( Chart II.2a ). Volatility in the WACR, as measured by the exponential weighted moving average (EWMA) 6 , declined considerably in the beginning of FY 2026-27, however, it increased marginally in July, and remained moderate till September ( Chart II.2b ). Reflecting the evolving liquidity conditions, the average spread of WACR over the policy repo rate turned positive during May-July 2026, before turning negative in August and plunging further in September ( Chart II.2b ). Overnight rates in the collateralised segment, i.e., triparty repo (TREPS) and market repo, broadly tracked the WACR, although both fell below the SDF rate intermittently during H1:2026-27 ( Chart II.3 ). Money market activity remained concentrated in the collateralised segments (tri-party and market repo), with their share in overnight money market volume at 97 per cent. During H1:2026-27, the share of the uncollateralised segment, i.e., the call money market, persisted around 3 per cent. Mutual funds remained the major lenders in tri-party repo with their share unchanged at 65 per cent in H1:2026-27, while their share in total lending in market repo segment moderated to 41 per cent in H1 from 48 per cent in H2:2025-26. The share of foreign banks in market repo lending increased to 31 per cent in H1:2026-27 from 29 per cent in H2:2025-26. On the borrowing side, public sector banks (PSBs) were the major player in tri-party repo, with their share increasing to 35 per cent in H1:2026-27 from 32 per cent in H2:2025-26. The share of private banks reduced noticeably to 14 per cent from 24 per cent. The share of PSBs in market repo increased by 5 percentage points to 13 per cent over the same period. The rates in term segments of the money market also moved in line with the evolving liquidity conditions and uncertainty (also see Box II.1 ). While 3-month treasury bill (T-Bill) rates moved largely in line with the policy repo rate, the rates on certificates of deposits (CDs) and commercial papers (CPs) edged up in May, but moderated since July notwithstanding intermittent spikes. The average spread of CDs and CPs over the policy repo rate widened to 135 bps and 155 bps in H1:2026-27 from 116 bps and 136 bps, respectively, in H2:2025-26. The average spread of T-Bills over the policy repo rate increased to 5 bps from 1 bp over the same period ( Chart II.3 ). Box II.1: Drivers of CD and CP Rate Spreads Rates on short-term instruments like Certificates of Deposit (CDs) and Commercial Papers (CPs) generally move in tandem with the policy repo rate but diverge at times reflecting broader liquidity conditions and funding pressures. Starting from Q3 of 2025-26, CD/CP rates hardened and remained elevated even as the monetary policy easing cycle continued. It resulted in widening of spread of CD/CP rates over the policy repo rate. Besides liquidity conditions and funding pressures, several other factors can cause CP and CD spreads to deviate from their long-run averages, including, policy uncertainty, monetary policy expectations and market-specific factors such as issuance patterns, calendar effects, and episodes of market stress (Priyadarshini et al., 2024, Anshul et al., 2025). To disentangle the respective contribution of various factors which are intertwined and may operate simultaneously, uncorrelated shocks are identified using historical decompositions within a VAR framework using monthly data. The following VAR specification is used. Where Y t includes the selected endogenous variables, X t contains the exogenous dummies and Pε t are the orthogonalised shocks. The variables are selected to capture the main channels, viz., banking system liquidity, funding conditions and policy uncertainty through which they can affect short-term funding costs, while avoiding overlap across closely related measures. 7 For CDs, the funding block also captures banks’ balance-sheet pressures through changes in outstanding credit-deposit ratio and net CD issuance growth. For CPs, only net issuance growth is used to capture funding conditions. The uncorrelated shocks are identified using a recursive identification scheme where the most exogenous factors are placed at the top while the response variable, i.e., CD or CP spreads are placed at the end of the ordering. Historical decomposition for the period January 2025 – July 2026 show the extent of contribution by each identified factor to the movements in spreads ( Chart II.1.1 ). The decomposition results suggest that the drivers of CD and CP spreads have shifted over time. Relatively tight liquidity conditions were the main driver of widening spreads during early 2025, but increased system liquidity along with policy rate easing led spreads to moderate to relatively lower levels by mid-2025. Since late 2025, the spreads hardened again. Funding pressures, owing to stronger credit growth relative to deposit mobilisation, contributed to hardening of CD spread, while economic policy uncertainty was the main driver of widening CP spread. More recently, idiosyncratic market-specific pressures have also contributed to the widening which are unrelated to the identified shocks in the model. II.2.3 Corporate Bond Market Corporate bond yields evolved in sync with G-sec yields with a hardening bias during H1:2026-27, while the risk premia showed mixed trends ( Chart II.10a ). The average bond market risk premium (i.e., the spread of 3-year AAA corporate bond yields over 3-year G-sec yields) hardened from 129 bps to 140 bps for NBFCs, and from 112 bps to 122 bps for corporates, but remained stable at 109 bps for Public Sector Units (PSUs), Financial Institutions (FIs) and banks in H1, even as corporate earnings remained robust in Q1 ( Chart II.10b and Table II.4 ). Primary issuances of listed corporate bonds in domestic markets declined by 17.9 per cent during H1:2026-27 (up to August 2026) as compared to the corresponding period of the previous year reflecting higher yields ( Chart II.11a ). Overseas issuances increased to ₹1,31,931 crore during H1:2026-27 (up to August 2026) from ₹10,303 crore during the same period last year, partly attributed to RBI’s swap facility. Most of the resource mobilisation in the corporate bond market (99 per cent) was through the private placement route. Outstanding investments by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) in corporate bonds stood at ₹2.7 lakh crore as at end-September, 2026 with utilisation of investment limits at 29.3 per cent ( Chart II.11b ). Trading volume in the secondary market moderated to ₹9.5 lakh crore during H1 (up to August 2026) from ₹10.1 lakh crore during the corresponding period of the previous year. II.2.5 Foreign Exchange Market The foreign exchange market remained volatile during H1:2026-27, driven by shifting US policies on tariff and policy rate, and lingering conflict in West Asia. While the rupee initially depreciated in the aftermath of the West Asia conflict, policy measures announced by the Reserve Bank and the Government to bolster capital flows arrested its decline. The implied volatility cooled down after peaking to a multi-year high in the wake of the West Asia conflict ( Chart II.15 ). Overall, the rupee depreciated by 1.4 per cent against the US dollar in H1:2026-27, a marked moderation from the sharp depreciation of 6.2 per cent witnessed in H2:2025-26 ( Chart II.16 ). The relative standing of the rupee among EM currencies also improved even as the pressures from volatile global market, elevated crude oil prices and the prolonged West Asia conflict weighed on the currency. Forward premia moderated during H1:2026-27 from the peak seen in the first week of April, supported by measures undertaken by the Government and the Reserve Bank to attract foreign capital. Upward pressures persisted, however, reflecting volatility in crude oil prices and flare-up of tensions in West Asia conflict ( Chart II.17 ). In terms of the 40-currency real effective exchange rate (REER), the INR depreciated by 0.5 per cent between March and August 2026, driven by the depreciation of the rupee in nominal terms ( Chart II.18a ). During the period, the movement in REER index was modest, as compared to major peer emerging economies ( Chart II.18b ). II.2.6 Bank and Non-Bank Credit Bank Credit: Aggregate Trends Bank credit growth strengthened further during H1: 2026–27 (up to September 15), on the back of robust loan demand ( Chart II.19 ). As on September 15, 2026, credit growth (y-o-y) for scheduled commercial banks (SCBs) accelerated sharply to 18.1 per cent, from 10.4 per cent during the corresponding period in the previous year ( Chart II.20 ). Across bank groups, foreign banks recorded the highest credit expansion at 25.8 per cent y-o-y, outperforming private banks (PVBs) at 19.1 per cent and public sector banks (PSBs) at 16.9 per cent. While PSBs contributed the largest share to y-o-y incremental credit, their overall market share contracted due to aggressive lending by both PVBs and foreign banks. The asset quality of SCBs strengthened further in Q1:2026-27 with the overall gross non-performing assets (NPA) ratio declining to 1.8 per cent in June 2026 from 2.3 per cent a year ago ( Chart II.21a ). The improvement spanned all major sectors, except for services and retail loans, where asset quality remained unchanged ( Chart II.21b ). Banks’ non statutory liquidity ratio (non-SLR) investments (comprising CPs, bonds, debentures, and shares of public and private corporates) increased by around 2.9 per cent during H1:2026-27 (up to September 15), with an increase in investments in commercial papers due to higher returns ( Chart II.22a ). Growth in adjusted non-food bank credit (i.e., non-food bank credit plus banks’ non-SLR investments) accelerated to 17.6 per cent (y-o-y) in Q2:2026-27 (up to September 15) from 10.1 per cent in Q2:2025-26, ( Chart II.22b ). As on August 31, 2026, excess holdings of SLR securities by SCBs marginally moderated to 6.3 per cent of their net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) from 6.4 per cent at end-March 2026 as banks brought down their investment portfolio to fund credit demand ( Chart II.23 ). Bank Credit: A Sectoral Perspective Sectoral trends 8 , 9 indicate strengthening of credit growth across major segments. Sustained robust economic activity continued to underpin credit demand, supporting broad-based expansion in bank credit. Monetary policy was found to have heterogenous impact on sectoral credit growth ( Box II.2 ). Box II.2: Bank Lending Channel of Monetary Policy: A Sectoral Approach Indian financial system continues to be bank-dominated. Bank credit as a proportion to GDP surged from 52.8 per cent in 2011-12 to 59.8 per cent in 2025-26. Therefore, given the importance of the banking sector, it becomes pertinent to understand the effectiveness of the transmission of monetary policy through the lending channel to various sectors of the economy. Under the current policy easing cycle, bank credit has inched up considerably across sectors. Demand conditions for credit have also been strong on the back of persisting buoyancy in domestic economic activity. In this milieu, it would be important to empirically decipher the response of sectoral bank credit to monetary policy shocks. Against this backdrop, the dynamic response of overall bank credit and credit to major sectors over 24 months following an unexpected policy rate change is examined using panel local projection technique (Jordà, 2005). Policy surprises are extracted using data on Overnight Index Swap (OIS) rates around RBI policy announcement dates, after controlling for current macroeconomic conditions (Lakdawala and Sengupta, 2025). Using monthly bank-level panel data of 40 banks for the period March 2014 - March 2026, the baseline specification for each horizon h = 0, 1, ..., 24 is given as under: Where, y i,t represents credit growth for bank i in time t, y i,t+h – y i,t–1 is the dependent variable representing the cumulative credit growth for bank i from the pre-shock period to horizon h, α i,h are bank fixed effects at horizon h, Shock t is the exogenous monetary policy (target factor) shock at time t, and β h is the coefficient of interest, capturing the cumulative impulse response of bank credit to a one standard deviation monetary policy shock at horizon h. Plotting β h for h = 0, 1, ..., 24 traces the impulse response function. Shock t–j are lagged shocks controlling for prior monetary policy actions, Δy i,t–j controls for lagged values of the dependent variable, credit growth, X i,t–1 is a vector of lagged bank characteristics (size, soundness, profitability, credit to deposits and borrowing ratio and asset quality) that can affect credit growth, MC t–p are lagged macroeconomic controls (nominal GDP growth and inflation) and D t and C t are dummies for demonetisation and COVID-19 pandemic, respectively. ε i,t+h is the idiosyncratic error term clustered at the bank level. The lag length (p) is set to 12 months following the documented 6-to-18-month transmission lag in the Indian banking sector (Khundrakpam and Jain, 2012; Raj, et al, 2020). The impulse response of aggregate non-food credit to a one standard deviation expansionary monetary policy shock indicates that credit expands over the short to medium term, increasing by approximately 0.50 percentage points (pp) within the first six months, peaking to 0.8 pp around 13 months after the shock but becomes insignificant by the 15th month. Credit growth increases immediately following expansionary monetary policy shocks, reaches a peak after one year, and gradually reverts as balance sheets adjust ( Chart II.2.1 ). Across major sectors, the impact of the expansionary monetary policy shock is found to be heterogeneous. Credit to agriculture sector remains steady initially, before expanding from around 4th month onwards, reaching the peak in around 18 months. Industry and services sectors respond immediately to the monetary policy shock, with industry reaching its peak expansion earlier (around 10 months) than services (around 13 months), after which both sectors’ responses gradually taper off. The response of personal loans is found to be delayed, remaining flat over the first few months, but it follows a steeper expansion and peaks around 10th month, like industry ( Chart II.2.2 ).
