V.3 Growth Outlook Domestic economic activity remains resilient supported by private consumption and fixed investment. High-capacity utilisation, robust bank credit growth, conducive financial conditions, and the government’s continued emphasis on infrastructure are expected to stimulate investment activity. Moreover, several measures announced in the Union Budget 2026-27 are also growth supportive. However, spillovers from heightened geopolitical tensions, along with volatility in international financial markets and trade dynamics, pose downside risks to the growth outlook. Forward-looking surveys offer additional insights. The bi-monthly consumer confidence (current situation index) for urban households remained almost at a similar level in September 2026 vis-à-vis the previous round. Consumer confidence of rural households registered a decline in the latest survey round, dipping further into pessimistic zone ( Chart V.7 ). Consumers’ optimism for the year ahead, measured by the future expectations index, remained in positive territory; however, it continued to decline for both urban and rural households in the recent survey round, driven mainly by lower expectations across most survey parameters ( Chart V.7 ). In the Reserve Bank’s quarterly industrial outlook survey of July-September 2026, manufacturing firms continued to stay optimistic and recorded improved sentiments of the firms from the previous quarter about the business conditions (BAI/BEI) 9 ( Chart V.8a ). The services firms experienced some moderation in sentiments in Q3:2026-27 as compared to previous quarter, while optimism increased for infrastructure firms ( Charts V.8b and V.8c ). Professional forecasters polled in the September 2026 round of the Reserve Bank’s survey expect real GDP growth to be at 7.2 per cent during Q2:2026-27. Growth is expected at about 6.8-7.1 per cent during the subsequent four quarters ( Chart V.9 ). Taking into account the baseline assumptions, survey indicators and model forecasts, real GDP growth is expected at 7.1 per cent in 2026-27 with 7.2 per cent in Q2; 6.9 per cent in Q3 and 6.8 per cent in Q4 – with risks evenly balanced around this baseline path ( Chart V.10 and Table V.3 ). Assuming a normal monsoon and no major exogenous or policy shocks, structural model estimates for 2027-28 place real GDP growth at 7.0 per cent. There are upside and downside risks to the baseline growth estimate. Upside risks emanate from easing of geopolitical tensions, abating of trade-related uncertainty and a broad-based revival in private investment. On the downside, spillovers from prolonged geopolitical tensions, volatility in global financial markets, shifting trade patterns, and climate-related shocks pose risks to the baseline growth path. V.4 Balance of Risks The baseline projections of domestic growth and inflation remain conditional on key domestic and global macroeconomic assumptions that are given in Table V.2 . These assumptions are subject to evolving uncertainties from ongoing geopolitical tensions in West Asia, commodity price volatility, global trade fragmentation, and domestic weather-related risks. Against this backdrop, this section outlines the balance of risks surrounding the baseline projections under plausible alternative scenarios. (i) Global Growth Uncertainties Global economic activity is navigating crosscurrents from ongoing war-induced supply shocks and a positive technology-led investment cycle. Growth momentum remains highly uneven, with advanced and emerging economies that are integrated into the artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor value chains experiencing technology-driven growth. In contrast, activity across energy-importing and non-tech economies are constrained by elevated energy prices, structural headwinds, and trade disruptions. Downside risks to global growth dominate. Broadening geopolitical conflicts in the West Asia may continue to disrupt global supply chains and critical maritime transit routes, particularly the Strait of Hormuz. This continued escalation of geopolitical hostilities may further disrupt the commodity markets. Moreover, elevated policy uncertainty and a potential surge in trade protectionism may restrain international trade flows and investment. High public debt levels in major economies leave sovereign markets exposed to financial tightening, restricting the fiscal space for productive investment. Downside risk also originate from potential sharp downside corrections in AI-related asset valuations which pose contagion risks to global financial markets. On the upside, a durable resolution of geopolitical tensions, swifter normalisation in energy markets, and faster AI-driven productivity gains could lift global growth above the baseline. If global growth turns out to be 100 bps below the baseline, domestic growth and inflation could be lower by around 30 bps and 15 bps, respectively. Conversely, if global growth is higher by 50 bps relative to the baseline, domestic growth and inflation could turn out to be higher by around 15 bps and 7 bps, respectively ( Charts V.11a and V.12a ). (ii) International Crude Oil Prices Global crude oil markets remain volatile due to supply disruptions in the Gulf region. After prices surged following the onset of the West Asia conflict, brent crude oil scaled a peak of US$105 per barrel in late July 2026 following renewed hostilities and maritime disruptions, before easing to around US$90 per barrel by end August 2026. Prices rose to an average of US$114 during September 2026. According to the Oil Market Report by International Energy Agency (IEA), approximately 10.0 million barrels per day (mb/d) of Gulf output remained unavailable as of August 2026. The IEA projects global oil supply to contract by 5.7 mb/d, while global oil demand is expected to decline by 2.5 mb/d in 2026. The primary upside risks originate from significant supply disruption due to prolonged West Asia conflict, which could threaten major energy infrastructure or further restrict critical maritime transit routes. Additionally, deeper, or prolonged production constraints by major oil-exporting nations, combined with depleted global inventory buffers, could severely tighten supply. If these shocks materialise, a sustained spike in crude oil prices would rapidly transmit to domestic inflation through higher imported fuel costs and second round effects ( Box V.1 ). Assuming full pass-through to domestic product prices, if crude oil prices are higher by 10 per cent than the baseline, inflation could turn out to be higher by around 50 bps and growth may be lower by around 15 bps. Conversely, sharper-than-expected deceleration in global growth, an accelerated resolution to ongoing geopolitical hostilities or robust production increases from non-traditional suppliers could ease prices. If crude oil prices are lower by 10 per cent relative to the baseline, inflation could be lower by around 50 bps and GDP growth could be higher by 15 bps ( Charts V.11a and V.12a ). Box V.1: Crude Oil Price Shocks: Quantifying the Macroeconomic Impact on the Indian Economy Being an energy importer, crude oil price dynamics remain a critical determinant of macroeconomic stability in India, exerting a profound influence on domestic price stability, external sector balances, and overall growth outlook. Global crude oil prices have experienced extreme volatility in 2026 so far, driven by the West Asian conflict and supply chain disruptions. The Indian crude oil basket spiked to around US$125 per barrel in March 2026. Prices subsequently eased to an average of US$82 per barrel in July, before rising to US$90 per barrel by August 2026. The renewed West Asia conflict has pushed up crude oil prices to $116 per barrel in September 2026. Given India’s heavy reliance on external energy sources, adverse international crude price shocks pose significant pass-through risks to headline inflation – both directly through fuel components and indirectly via generalised cost-push pressures, creating headwinds to medium-term macroeconomic stability. Furthermore, the broader global energy outlook remains clouded by several compounding factors including widespread uncertainty regarding the timeline for supply resumption and the restoration of critical shipping routes. Additionally, global strategic petroleum reserves remain low, leaving markets vulnerable to further shocks. To evaluate how these price fluctuations ripple through the economy, the Quarterly Projection Model (QPM) is utilised to delineate several interconnected channels through which the increase in crude oil prices impacts the economy (John et.al., 2022, 2023). An escalation in crude oil prices adversely impacts key global macroeconomic aggregates, aggravating global inflationary pressures, dampening output growth, possibly triggering higher monetary policy rates. Heightened global energy prices cause import bill to rise, putting downward pressure on the domestic currency, leading to rise in imported inflation. An immediate pass-through of international price movements to domestic energy prices exert an instantaneous upward pressure on headline inflation, capturing the direct effect. The increase in petroleum product prices triggers indirect cost push effects emanating from firms passing on higher input costs, pushing up prices of final goods and services. Concurrently, elevated energy prices compress household real disposable incomes and narrow corporate profit margins, precipitating a contraction in discretionary consumer spending and private investment. This resultant moderation in aggregate demand has a dampening effect on inflationary pressures. To prevent inflation expectations from getting unhinged, the central bank could raise policy rates. This monetary tightening widens the output gap and compresses demand to bring inflation back to target. Chart V.1.1 depicts the decomposition of impact on headline inflation due to a persistent 10 per cent shock in crude oil prices highlighting the relative strength of the channels of transmission. Higher inflation in the first year is primarily driven by the direct effects, which dissipates over the next year. In the medium term, indirect cost push effects play the prominent role. While the demand channel exerts a moderating impact on price pressures, its offsetting impact is considerably smaller than that of the cost-push channel. Furthermore, monetary policy reaction also imparts a consequential dampening effect on inflation in the medium-term. In the case of output growth, the favourable impact of exchange rate depreciation will only be evident in the first year but this impact will be more than offset by moderation in domestic demand as well as weaker global growth. The pass-through of a depreciated currency turns contractionary in the subsequent year, as higher imported costs exert pressure on macroeconomic output ( Chart V.1.2 ). References: John, J., Kumar, D., George, A.T., Mitra, P., Kapur, M. and Patra. M.D. (2023), “A Recalibrated Quarterly Projection Model (QPM 2.0) for India”, Reserve Bank of India Bulletin, February, pp.59-77. John, J., Kumar, D., and Patra, M.D. (2022). Monetary Policy: Confronting Supply-driven Inflation, Reserve Bank of India Bulletin, July, pp. 97-109. (iii) Exchange Rate The Indian Rupee (INR) was supported by robust FCNR(B) deposit inflows in early September 2026, subsequently, these gains were reversed due to higher crude oil prices. Looking ahead, the INR may face headwinds, including a robust US dollar, elevated import cost, volatile capital inflows and rise in trade policy uncertainties. Any escalation in geopolitical tensions or unexpectedly aggressive monetary tightening by major central banks may put pressure on INR. Conversely, the INR could find support from the resilience of India’s services exports, the stability in bilateral trade frameworks and sustained foreign capital inflows. In a scenario where the INR depreciates by 5 per cent over the baseline, inflation could be higher by around 40 bps, while GDP growth may benefit by around 25 bps through the exports channel in the short term, under normal macroeconomic conditions. In contrast, an appreciation of the INR by 5 per cent relative to the baseline would moderate both inflation and GDP growth by around 40 bps and 25 bps, respectively ( Charts V.11b and V.12b ). (iv) Food Inflation Domestic headline CPI inflation experienced an uptick in mid-2026, driven primarily by food price pressures. Price pressures across all the classes within the food and beverage basket firmed up. Risk to agricultural crops remain in the wake of deficient and erratic monsoon experienced in 2026-27. Food price risks remain sensitive to weather variations. Adverse impact of El Niño, unseasonal rain, lower reservoir levels, localised heatwaves, higher input costs pose upside risks to food inflation, which may result in headline inflation being higher by 40 bps vis-à-vis the baseline. On the other hand, large buffer stocks, and government's various supply side measures could moderate headline inflation by around 40 bps relative to the baseline ( Charts V.11b and V.12b ). V.5 Conclusion India’s macroeconomic outlook continues to be supported by resilient domestic economic activity on the back of private consumption and investment. The external environment, however, remains uncertain. At the same time, improving investment outlook, bilateral trade agreements and conducive financial conditions could provide further support to economic activity. On the inflation front, the recent increase in headline inflation has been driven largely by food and fuel prices, but core inflation has also registered a pickup from its benign levels, indicating signs of greater generalisation of price pressures as evident from diffusion indices. Going forward, upside risks to the inflation outlook persist from renewed geopolitical tensions, disruptions to energy supplies and adverse weather conditions. Against this backdrop, potential second-round effects warrant stricter vigilance particularly as demand conditions remain strong. Overall, the outlook for growth and inflation will depend on how domestic demand and supply conditions evolve alongside developments in the global economy, with the balance of risks remaining contingent on these factors. _________________________________________________________________________________ 1 World Economic Outlook (WEO) Update, International Monetary Fund (IMF), July 2026. 2 The Reserve Bank’s inflation expectations survey of households is being conducted in 19 cities since March 2021 (18 cities in the previous rounds) and the results of the September 2026 round are based on responses from 5,987 households. 3 The Reserve Bank’s rural consumer confidence survey is being conducted across all Indian states and three major UTs since September 2023 and the results of the September 2026 round are based on responses from 8,799 respondents. 4 The results of the July-September 2026 round of the industrial outlook survey are based on responses from 1,224 companies. 5 Based on 666 services companies and 84 infrastructure firms polled in the July-September 2026 round of the services and infrastructure outlook survey. 6 Forty-seven panellists participated in the September 2026 round of the Reserve Bank’s Survey of Professional Forecasters. 7 ‘Fuel’ represents two categories, viz., ‘electricity, gas and other fuels’; and ‘Fuels and lubricants for personal transport equipment’ which includes ‘petrol’, ‘diesel’, and ‘other natural gas (CNG)’. 8 Joice John, Deepak Kumar, Asish Thomas George, Pratik Mitra, Muneesh Kapur and Michael Debabrata Patra (2023), “A Recalibrated Quarterly Projection Model (QPM 2.0) for India”, Reserve Bank of India Bulletin, February, Volume LXXVII (2), pp.59-77. 9 Business Assessment Index (BAI)/Business Expectations Index (BEI) (over a range of 0 to 200) gives a snapshot of demand conditions in the manufacturing sector by combining nine parameters – (i) overall business situation, (ii) production, (iii) order books, (iv) inventory of raw material, (v) inventory of finished goods, (vi) profit margin, (vii) employment, (viii) exports and (ix) capacity utilisation. A value above 100 indicates an expansion of the overall business activity and value below 100 indicates contraction. Monetary Policy Report – October 2026

Disentangling Demand and Supply Factors Chapter V: Macroeconomic Outlook V.1: Key Developments since the April 2026 MPR V.2: Inflation Outlook V.3: Growth Outlook V.4: Balance of Risks V.5: Conclusion Box V.1: Crude Oil Price Shocks: Quantifying the Macroeconomic Impact on the Indian Economy Abbreviations Executive Summary Global growth remained resilient in 2026 so far, supported by AI-related investment, and fiscal stimulus measures, despite disruptions due to the ongoing West Asia conflict. Renewed energy-price pressures stoked inflation pressures and prompted a more hawkish stance from leading central bank. Fiscal sustainability concerns, persistent inflation, and geopolitical uncertainty raised bond yields, while equity markets remained volatile amid lingering concern on valuations technology stocks. Amidst global uncertainty, domestic financial markets underwent intermittent volatility during H1:2026-27. System liquidity surplus surged in September 2026, mainly on account of the Reserve Bank’s swap facilities. Overnight rates in the money market evolved in sync with prevailing liquidity conditions. Transmission to lending

and deposit rates plateaued with status quo in policy rate during H1:2026-27. Bank credit growth became broad based and strengthened further. The domestic economy showed resilience in H1:2026-27, despite continued global uncertainty amidst the conflict. The supply-side pressures were alleviated by proactive policy measures by the government that ensured adequate supply of key inputs. Real GDP recorded a growth of 7.8 per cent in Q1:2026-27 reflecting strong momentum in underlying economic activity. Aggregate demand remained strong on the back of both private consumption and investment. Net external demand was also robust and contributed significantly to growth. On the supply side, both manufacturing and services sectors recorded strong growth in Q1. High frequency indicators suggest continued buoyancy in domestic economic activity, albeit with some moderation compared to Q1. Stable employment conditions, congenial financial conditions, revival in corporate investment, and a pickup in goods exports – nurtured by bilateral FTAs and diversification – are expected to support economic activity going forward. Sustenance of private consumption growth will be essential for broad-based recovery in private capex. Headline CPI inflation increased sequentially, rising above the target during June-August, driven by a sustained positive price momentum. Food and fuel groups led to this increase, reflecting adverse weather conditions and the sharp rise in energy prices following the West Asia conflict. Core inflation registered a pick-up with some signs of generalisation in recent months. Input cost pressures have accentuated, but the pass-through has remained limited so far. Going forward, India’s macroeconomic outlook remains resilient supported by domestic demand and strengthening investment, despite persistent global uncertainties. The outlook remains vulnerable to geopolitical developments, volatility in global energy markets and weather-related uncertainties. Weak monsoons coupled with strong El Niño, protracted geopolitical tensions, rising international commodity prices, additional frictions in global trade and tightening of global financial conditions could

adversely impact the growth outlook. Persistent supply-side pressures in food and volatile global energy prices pose risks to the domestic inflation outlook, particularly through second-round effects amid strong growth impulses. The interplay of these factors will shape the evolving growth–inflation dynamics, with the balance of risks depending on developments in global growth, crude oil prices, exchange-rate movements, and domestic food supplies. I. External Environment Global growth remains resilient, mainly supported by AI-related investment and fiscal measures, but faces renewed supply-side shocks from the West Asia conflict, elevated oil prices and trade related frictions. Inflation has accelerated again, prompting central banks to shift towards a more cautious and hawkish monetary policy stance. Financial markets remain volatile amid higher yields, geopolitical tensions and shifting risk sentiment. Global growth has remained resilient despite facing persistent headwinds from supply shocks. However, the near-term growth forecasts have been revised downwards by several multilateral agencies, as key supply chains remain disrupted and crude oil prices remain elevated. Investment in artificial intelligence (AI) and related technologies, along with increased international trade in AI-related hardware, has supported global economic activity. Fiscal support across countries has sustained economic activity but also heightened concerns about rising public debt and reduced fiscal buffers. Along with higher inflation and higher-for-longer monetary policy expectations, these concerns have contributed to a sharp rise in government bond yields across major jurisdictions. Inflation, which had been moderating towards the end of 2025, began to accelerate following the supply shock triggered by the West Asia conflict. Crude oil prices rose to levels not seen in recent years. At the same time, other commodity prices also increased, feeding into higher goods inflation even as services inflation remained elevated in several major economies. Consequently, central banks that had been moving towards monetary policy normalisation last year adopted a more

hawkish stance following the onset of the conflict. Several advanced and emerging market economies (EMEs) have tightened monetary policy or maintained a cautious stance, while only a handful have reduced policy rates to support growth. Of late, the US Fed and the European Central Bank (ECB) have been placing greater emphasis on incoming data and their monetary policy frameworks in decision making, rather than on forward guidance. The Fed’s hawkish stance, combined with elevated crude oil prices, contributed to risk-off sentiment and portfolio outflows from EMEs, exerting depreciation pressure on their currencies. Sovereign bond yields have hardened globally, particularly in advanced economies (AEs), on concerns over rising public debt, debt-servicing costs and persistent inflation concerns. Emerging market equities experienced selloffs during Q3 of 2026, with some recovery in August while advanced economy equities gained, driven by technology stocks and healthy corporate profits. The US dollar gained, as higher bond yields, expectations of a hawkish Fed, and safe-haven demand amid geopolitical uncertainty outweighed intermittent weakness. I.1 Global Economic Conditions In 2026 so far, global growth has remained resilient, even as near-term growth forecasts have been revised downwards amid the fragile geopolitical situation in West Asia. The growth outlook is dependent on the de-escalation of the conflict, as key supply chains continue to face disruptions, and oil prices remain elevated. In its July 2026 World Economic Outlook update, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) lowered its global growth projection for 2026 by 10 bps to 3.0 per cent, reflecting the uncertainty around the outlook. However, it raised its projection by 20 bps for 2027 to 3.4 per cent, as the impact of the conflict remains less than what was anticipated earlier, while AI-related investment and productivity gains are likely to fuel growth. Meanwhile, the OECD, in its September 2026 Interim Economic Outlook, marginally

raised its global growth forecast by 10 bps to 2.9 per cent for 2026, while lowering its 2027 projection by 10 bps to 3.0 per cent. While AI-related activity is expected to provide continued support, stronger price pressures and elevated interest rates are likely to weigh on near-term growth momentum. Among AEs, real GDP growth in the US remained resilient in 2026, supported by robust consumer spending and investment, including continued private investment in AI and related technologies. Growth, however, moderated in the second quarter, reflecting a downturn in government spending, slower investment and export growth, while stronger consumer spending partly offset these effects ( Table I.1 ). Since April 2026, labour market conditions have softened, with non-farm payroll growth slowing down during summer and weakening further in September, while the unemployment rate remained largely stable. The composite PMI continued to expand strongly in August, recording a 52-month high, driven by services while manufacturing remained healthy amid improved business optimism and new orders. Consumer sentiment, as measured by the University of Michigan Survey, declined in September to its lowest level in four months, amid growing concerns about elevated prices. Overall, underlying economic activity in the US remains resilient. Among other AEs, growth in Japan in 2026 so far has been largely driven by the external sector. GDP growth strengthened in Q1, with net exports making the largest contribution. Growth moderated in Q2 due to slowdown in domestic demand, particularly private investment, though this moderation was offset largely by a strong contribution from net exports. The composite PMI continued to expand in August, driven by manufacturing while services also improved. On the other hand, GDP growth recovered in the euro area in Q2 after stagnating in Q1, primarily driven by strong growth in Ireland and Spain. Household and government expenditure continued

to provide support to economic activity. The composite PMI expanded in August at the same pace for the second consecutive month as the moderation in services was offset by solid expansion in manufacturing amid growth in new orders and factory output. In the UK, GDP growth rebounded in Q1 2026, supported by services and broad-based expansion across the economy, with gross capital formation and household consumption driving growth on the expenditure side. Growth moderated in Q2, reflecting weaker household consumption and lower inventory accumulation amid the adverse effects of the conflict in West Asia. Among high-frequency indicators, the composite PMI expanded in August for the second consecutive month, driven by services sector activity offsetting the moderation in manufacturing. taken from the IMF WEO, July 2026 update. Sources: Official statistical agencies; Bloomberg; and IMF. Among major EMEs, China’s growth is facing challenges from subdued consumption and a weaker external sector in 2026, with GDP growth moderating in Q2 from Q1. The composition of growth has also undergone a shift, with the share of net exports in GDP growth declining significantly relative to 2025, while the share of gross capital formation increased. Investment growth remains uneven, with stronger activity concentrated in AI-related and high-tech sectors. High-frequency indicators also point to subdued activity, with composite PMI slowing in July as both manufacturing and services sector activity moderated. In August, however, PMI rebounded as output and new orders increased in both the sectors but remained below the average for 2026. Brazil’s GDP growth remained stable at 1.8 per cent (y-o-y) in Q1, marking the third consecutive quarter of growth at this pace. The agriculture and services sectors supported growth while industrial activity declined. In Q2, however, GDP expanded by 2.0 per cent, driven by recovery in industrial sector and sustained growth in agriculture. Industrial sector benefited from higher oil and gas extraction amid higher energy prices. Brazil’s composite PMI remained very close to the neutral line in the last few months, reflecting weakness in the economy as new orders continue to fall. Russia’s economy contracted in Q1, reflecting weak manufacturing and construction activity, although services remained resilient. Activity recovered in Q2, led by manufacturing, while agriculture remained subdued. The composite PMI also returned to expansion in August, ending five consecutive months of contraction, supported by stronger output and new orders. In South Africa, GDP growth accelerated in Q1, driven by a recovery in agriculture, increased mining activity, and stronger momentum in services, before moderating in Q2 led by a contraction in manufacturing

and mining. Composite PMI continued to remain around neutral line in August amidst subdued new orders and weak business confidence. The Asian Development Bank (ADB), in its September 2026 outlook, projected ASEAN 1 growth at 4.7 per cent in both 2026 and 2027. The outlook remains subject to downside risks from the West Asia conflict, elevated energy and commodity prices, weaker external demand and heightened global uncertainty. Turning to high-frequency indicators, the OECD’s composite leading indicators (CLIs) showed that most economies remained above their long-term trend in Q2 and Q3 (till August) of 2026 ( Chart I.1a ). The global composite PMI expanded at its quickest pace in August in more than two years, with broad-based expansion in both output and new orders ( Chart I.1b ). The services sector continued to expand in August for the fifth straight month, while the manufacturing sector remained solid. World merchandise trade expanded for eleven consecutive quarters through Q2:2026, with growth remaining robust and exceeding expectations. Both EMEs and AEs contributed to the expansion, though the impulse came largely from EMEs, with moderation in contribution by the AEs as frontloading of US imports moderated. In July 2026, world merchandise trade volume growth remained strong at 6.0 per cent (y-o-y), with EMEs contributing 3.2 percentage points and AEs 2.8 percentage points ( Chart I.2a ). The surge in trade of electronic components related to AI offset the negative impact of the conflict in West Asia. The WTO, in its March 2026 update, revised its projection for global merchandise trade volume growth from 0.5 per cent to 1.9 per cent in 2026, reflecting strong AI-related trade and a smaller-than-anticipated impact of tariffs. The Goods Trade Barometer (September 2026, WTO) remained above trend at 102.0, with the electronic components and other goods linked to investment in

artificial intelligence (AI) indices indicating continued momentum in merchandise trade. Meanwhile, shipping costs remained elevated, with the Freightos Baltic Global Index staying higher in 2026 - above its 2025 average - reflecting the rerouting of vessels away from disrupted shipping corridors/chokepoints and continued capacity pressures ( Chart I.2b ). I.2 Commodity Prices and Inflation Commodity prices, as captured by the Bloomberg Commodity Index, have exhibited divergent movements, largely attributable to sector-specific fundamentals ( Chart I.3a ). Agricultural commodity prices have risen due to conflict-related disruptions to energy, fertiliser and shipping markets, adverse weather conditions and tighter crop-supply prospects. Global food prices, as reflected in the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) food price index, have increased since April 2026, mainly due to vegetable oils, cereals, and sugar ( Chart I.3b ). Gold prices declined through Q2 2026 amid expectations of higher interest rates. Gold prices gained overall in Q3 as heightened geopolitical uncertainty, including renewed tensions in West Asia, boosted safe-haven demand. Periods of weakness in the US dollar and lower expectations of further tightening by the Fed also supported prices, outweighing the drag from rising bond yields and the stronger dollar in September. Among base metals, copper and zinc prices have continued to rise, supported by tightening supply conditions. Aluminium prices rose to a four-year high in early June amid concerns over supply disruptions from the West Asia conflict, before moderating as the US dollar strengthened and Chinese exports increased ( Chart I.3c ). Energy prices surged in April, largely reflecting the sharp increase in Brent prices, before moderating as supply disruptions eased. However, the re-escalation of tensions in West Asia led to a renewed increase in energy prices in August and September, amid concerns over disruptions in regional oil production and shipping ( Chart I.4a ). Against this backdrop,

developments in global oil supply buffers and demand conditions remain important. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) is currently placed at roughly 284 million barrels, at its lowest level since October 1982. Strategic releases and inventory drawdowns helped to cushion shocks. Also, weaker import demand by China due to release of stocks and domestic demand destruction helped offset some supply pressures. However, if the disruptions last longer, there is lower flexibility available to deal with supply shortages ( Chart I.4 b&c ). Consumer Price Inflation Inflationary pressures have re-emerged following a temporary moderation, driven primarily by renewed energy and commodity price pressures amid heightened West Asia tensions. The US personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation metric, saw inflation surge through May, driven by a sharp increase in gasoline prices before falling subsequently as energy prices stabilised. In the UK, headline inflation has been lower in Q2 2026, mainly due to easing food inflation, before edging up in Q3 so far on rising energy and housing prices. In the euro area, energy prices and persistently high service inflation drove the CPI inflation higher, except for a modest correction in June due to a reversal in crude prices. In Japan, inflation rose steadily from April, reflecting a slower decline in energy prices as subsidies were scaled back in Q2, alongside imported inflation from yen depreciation. Inflation rose further in Q3, on elevated food prices and transportation costs, despite lower electricity prices. In EMEs, inflation has been divergent, reflecting differences in domestic demand conditions and supply-side pressures across economies. In Brazil, the headline CPI rose due to food and beverages, then fell as food, transport, and housing prices moderated. Inflation in South Africa accelerated from April to June, driven predominantly by higher fuel and transport costs, before easing

in July as fuel prices declined and food-price inflation moderated. In Russia, CPI inflation eased until May on easing food pressures before edging higher due to fuel and a weaker rouble. China’s CPI inflation has remained subdued, supported by persistent food-price deflation ( Chart I.5b ). I.3 Monetary Policy Stance Since April 2026, monetary policy actions have diverged across economies. However, major advanced economy central banks turned more hawkish in Q3 2026, as renewed West Asia tensions raised energy prices and intensified inflationary pressures. Among major AEs, the US Fed held the target range at 3.50–3.75 per cent through July. In September, amidst persistent inflationary pressures, robust economic activity and stable labour-market conditions, the Fed unanimously raised the target range by 25 basis points to 3.75–4.00 per cent. The Bank of England has maintained the policy rate unchanged at 3.75 per cent in the last six meetings, noting little evidence so far of material second-round effects from the energy shocks while reiterating that future policy decisions depend on how the energy shock evolves and its impact on inflation. The ECB raised its key policy rates by 25 basis points in June and again in September, taking the deposit facility rate to 2.50 per cent. The decisions reflected persistent energy-driven inflation pressures associated with the conflict; however, indirect and second-round effects have remained largely contained. The Bank of Japan (BoJ) continued policy normalisation, raising its policy rate by 25 basis points each in June and September to 1.25 per cent. The moves reflected persistent inflationary pressures, owing to higher import costs amid yen depreciation, with future policy decisions to be guided by developments in economic activity and prices. The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates in May amid elevated inflation and capacity pressures, and again in September as fuel-price pass-through and

stronger-than-expected growth intensified inflation risks. The Bank of Canada maintained status quo as longer-term inflation expectations have remained anchored and there was little evidence that oil prices had fed through more broadly to goods and services prices. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand hiked the policy rate by 25 bps for the first time in three years in July and then again in September by the same magnitude to 2.75 per cent. The monetary policy committee considered gradual withdrawal of monetary stimulus as appropriate to steer inflation to the 2 per cent target, while supporting growth and employment ( Chart I.6a ). Among key EMEs, Brazil continued its monetary easing cycle, with the central bank reducing the Selic rate in successive meetings amid signs of moderating economic activity and easing inflationary pressures. The Bank of Russia has gradually reduced its key rate as economic growth edged lower. China has held its benchmark rate at 3.0 per cent for more than a year amid ample liquidity. South Africa raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 7.25 per cent in September, following a similar increase in May, amid rising inflation risks and concerns over potential second-round effects. The Bank of Thailand kept its policy rate unchanged, balancing weaker growth and subdued domestic demand against conflict-related, supply-driven inflation pressures. The Bank of Mexico cut its policy rate by 25 basis points to 6.5 per cent in May, marking the end of its easing cycle. In September, it kept rates unchanged but removed its earlier forward guidance, signalling greater policy flexibility ( Chart I.6b ). I.4 Financial Markets Global financial markets remained largely resilient yet volatile, guided by the interplay of AI-driven risk appetite, shifting monetary policy expectations, elevated sovereign borrowing needs, and persistent geopolitical tensions in West Asia. The stock-bond correlation

in the AEs has shifted for the first time in decades, reflecting uncertainty due to supply-side shocks ( Box I.1 ). Box I.1: Stock–Bond Correlation in Advanced and Emerging Economies The equity–government bond return correlation is central to multi-asset portfolio diversification. Stock–bond return correlation is influenced by short-term rates, inflation, volatility, and economic growth (Aslanidis and Christiansen, 2012). Theoretical explanations link asset-price co-movement to macroeconomic conditions (Campbell et al., 2020), while changes in stock–bond correlation have important implications for portfolio diversification (Brixton et al., 2023). More recently, evidence from G7 economies suggests that the macroeconomic drivers of stock–bond correlation vary over time, with significant implications for portfolio risk and diversification (McMillan, 2026). After two decades of generally positive readings, the correlation in advanced economies turned sharply negative during the 2021–22 inflation surge and again in 2025 ( Chart I.1a ). Using a DCC-GARCH model, the analysis finds that stock–bond correlation in advanced economies follows an inflation-regime relationship. Inflation enters with a negative linear and positive quadratic term, implying that correlation is lowest near the inflation target and rises as inflation moves away from it ( Chart I.1b ). The implied turning point is 1.6 per cent, essentially at the 2 per cent target, and the real short rate is also positive and significant. The findings suggest that when inflation is moderate, government bonds tend to hedge equity-market risk. This mechanism, however, does not extend to emerging markets. Their correlation averages around +0.6 and never turns negative over the sample, while its relationship with domestic inflation is weak and statistically insignificant. A formal Wald test also rejects equality of the advanced- and emerging-market coefficients. Instead, global equity volatility (VIX) is the only significant explanatory variable. The results suggest that emerging-market government bonds behave more like risk assets than domestic safe havens,

selling off alongside equities when global risk appetite deteriorates. Thus, their diversification benefits are not evident in the post-2008 sample, unlike in advanced economies. References: 1. Global equities advanced in Q2 2026, driven by continued momentum in artificial intelligence (AI) and related capital investment cycles ( Chart I.7a ). Geopolitical tensions in West Asia added sporadic volatility during the quarter. The announcement of a US–Iran ceasefire framework and a memorandum of understanding (MoU) eased concerns about a broader regional conflict. Energy prices recoiled, and investor sentiment improved as fears of a sustained disruption to global energy supplies diminished. During Q2, US equities advanced, supported by resilient corporate earnings and sustained investor enthusiasm for AI-related companies. In the euro area, equities posted solid gains, with IT outperforming amid strong corporate earnings and diversification by investors from US markets. In the UK, equity prices rose, although declines in energy stocks limited overall gains. Markets largely looked through domestic political developments, with investor sentiment remaining broadly resilient. Japanese equities delivered robust returns in Q2 as easing tensions in West Asia buoyed sentiment, while the yen – at a four-decade low against the US dollar – supported exporters. In Q3, major equity markets posted modest gains, although investor

sentiment remained cautious amid expectations of further monetary tightening, elevated technology-sector valuations, and persisting tensions in West Asia. Equities gained in the US, supported by resilient corporate earnings and sustained AI optimism, with further support from the Fed’s commitment to combating inflation despite its hawkish stance. Euro-area equities declined in Q3 as higher energy prices and persistent inflation lifted bond yields and weighed on risk sentiment, while political uncertainty and fiscal concerns, added to investor caution. Japanese equities were affected by the global correction in AI-related stocks and also concerns surrounding a stronger yen which could weigh on exports. In the UK, equities made modest gains, supported by robust corporate earnings, and elevated commodity prices. Equity markets in most EMEs rose sharply in Q2:2026, outperforming global peers. Taiwan and Korea led market performance, driven by gains in memory and semiconductor stocks amid strong AI demand ( Chart I.7b ). In Q3, emerging-market equities surrendered the gains recorded in the previous quarter as the AI-led rally showed signs of fatigue. Renewed conflict in West Asia, heightened trade tensions, and expectations of a more hawkish Fed weighed on investor risk appetite. A global sell-off in government debt led by inflation persistence and high government deficits has raised borrowing costs. These pressures have been exacerbated by the West Asia conflict, which has driven up oil prices, leading investors to seek higher bond yields as the odds of rate cuts have largely diminished. Sovereign bond-market performance diverged in Q2: Japanese and US rates firmed up, while German and UK yields softened. Developments in West Asia continued to be a major driver of the market, with bond yields moving in tandem with oil prices. Yields on government bonds surged to multi-year highs around the middle of the quarter amid fears of further escalation but fell

on signs of a possible US–Iran deal. In the US, rates were underpinned by a resilient labour market and elevated government debt, reinforcing expectations that monetary policy would remain tight. A combination of global inflation concerns, and domestic politics hit UK gilts. In April, the 10-year gilt yield hit its highest level since 2008, reflecting inflationary pressures from higher oil prices and concerns about budgetary and political vulnerabilities ahead of municipal elections. Higher oil costs and imported-inflation pressures from the yen supported expectations for BoJ policy hikes this year, while concerns about fiscal expansion contributed to upside pressure. In Q3, government bond yields in major AEs have risen amid persistent energy-price pressures and tighter monetary policy, while elevated public debt and renewed fiscal support have added to upward pressure on long-term yields. In the US, higher oil prices, persistent inflation concerns, and higher borrowing requirements pushed treasury yields higher. The Treasury’s decision in mid-August to expand buybacks of long-dated securities provided only temporary relief, as underlying inflation and term-premium pressures continued to weigh on the market. Elsewhere, government bond yields in the euro area, Japan and the UK moved up amid renewed inflation concerns from rising energy prices, while rate hikes and firm policy signals, along with country-specific fiscal risks and elevated sovereign borrowing requirements, added to the rise in yields ( Chart I.8 a ). Emerging-market 10-year sovereign bonds recorded a mixed performance, displaying divergent country-specific inflation, fiscal, and monetary policy dynamics. While favourable risk sentiment and easing expectations initially supported some markets, the subsequent rise in oil prices, US sovereign bond yields, and geopolitical tensions tightened external financing conditions, increasing borrowing costs and weighing more heavily on sovereigns vulnerable to fiscal and external risks ( Chart I.8b ). In currency markets, the US dollar strengthened in Q2 2026,

supported by higher oil prices, heightened geopolitical tensions and still elevated inflation, which reinforced safe-haven demand and expectations of relatively tighter monetary policy. Most major currencies weakened against the US dollar, with the yen declining to a four-decade low despite large scale coordinated intervention by the US and the Bank of Japan. The euro also depreciated, while sterling demonstrated greater resilience. In Q3, the US dollar, which had remained broadly weak through much of the quarter, strengthened markedly in September. The rebound was driven by higher US bond yields and a repricing of expectations for further Fed tightening following the release of data suggesting resilient activity and persistent inflation concerns. Renewed geopolitical tensions in West Asia, elevated oil prices, and trade-related uncertainty also supported safe-haven demand for the dollar. Consequently, the dollar index rose by around 2.0 per cent during September to a near two-month high, although it ended Q3 only marginally higher. Against this backdrop, the renewed negative correlation between the S&P 500 and the US dollar since April indicates that the dollar has again provided a partial hedge during periods of equity-market stress, appreciating when risk sentiment deteriorated and weakening as risk appetite recovered ( Chart I.9 ). Shifts in monetary policy expectations, geopolitical developments, and global risk appetite can, however, quickly alter the stock–dollar correlation. The MSCI EM Currency Index rose driven by carry-seeking flows, supportive commodity prices and country-specific inflows. However, gains moderated late in the period amid renewed pressure from rising long-term US bond yields ( Chart I.10 a & b ). I.5 Conclusion The global economic outlook continues to be shaped by supply-side shocks emanating from the West Asia crisis, shifting trade tariffs, and the ongoing AI investment boom. Despite multilateral agencies projecting slower global growth in 2026, high-frequency indicators, including purchasing managers’ indices,

point to resilient economic activity. Inflation has picked up in most economies, prompting central banks to adopt a more hawkish stance. Long-term bond yields have risen amid persistent inflation concerns, while equity markets have advanced, underpinned by the ongoing AI-driven investment boom. II. Liquidity Conditions and Financial Markets System liquidity surplus surged during H1:2026-27 mainly on account of the Reserve Bank’s swap facilities. Overnight rates in the money market evolved in sync with prevailing liquidity conditions. Domestic financial markets exhibited two-way movements amidst global uncertainty. Transmission to lending rates moderated with status quo on policy rate since February 2026. Bank credit growth accelerated further. Sectoral trends indicate broad-based credit expansion. Introduction Global financial markets remained volatile amidst shifting expectations, persistent tensions in West Asia and rising fiscal concerns. Against this backdrop, domestic financial markets displayed intermittent volatility during H1:2026-27. System-wide liquidity surplus surged in September 2026 reflecting buoyant capital flows under the Reserve Bank’s swap facilities. Money market rates largely moved in line with the evolving liquidity conditions, with rates in Certificates of Deposit (CDs) and Commercial Papers (CPs) easing in Q2. The exchange rate exhibited two-way movements in H1. Monetary policy transmission to lending rate moderated during H1 amidst rate pause and funding pressure. Nonetheless, bank credit continued to grow robustly and financing from non-bank sources also increased. II.1 Liquidity Conditions and the Operating Procedure of Monetary Policy The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Act, 1934 requires the Reserve Bank to place the operating procedure relating to the implementation of monetary policy and changes thereto from time

to time, if any, in the public domain. 1 During H1:2026-27, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) kept the policy rate unchanged in three successive meetings while retaining the neutral policy stance. Drivers and Management of Liquidity System liquidity, as measured by the net balances under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF), improved significantly in H1:2026–27 from a moderate surplus in H2:2025–26 ( Chart II.1 ). On a net basis, average daily absorption under the LAF increased to ₹3.21 lakh crore in H1:2026–27 from ₹1.43 lakh crore in H2:2025–26. Capital inflows and the build-up of government cash balances were the principal drivers of liquidity conditions in H1:2026–27. System liquidity remained in surplus during H1:2026-27 except for end-June when it briefly turned into deficit amidst tax related outflows. 2 In Q1, liquidity conditions improved initially supported by faster government spending, but it moderated thereafter due to increase in currency in circulation (CiC) and the RBI’s foreign exchange operations. Liquidity conditions improved in Q2, aided by capital inflows under the RBI's swap facilities ( Table II.1 ). With liquidity conditions remaining largely in surplus, banks’ recourse to the marginal standing facility (MSF) averaged ₹0.01 lakh crore during H1:2026-27, while average daily standing deposit facility (SDF) balances increased marginally 3 . The Reserve Bank remained nimble and agile in its liquidity management operations, ensuring sufficient liquidity in the banking system to support transmission to money market. With surge in liquidity surplus mainly due to FCNR(B) swaps 4 , the RBI conducted variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) operations of varying maturities, although several variable rate repo (VRR) operations were also undertaken mainly until July 2026 to tide over transient liquidity tightness and align overnight rates with the policy rate. Overall, the RBI conducted a total of 36 VRR and 51 VRRR auctions in H1. On a

As on September 15, 2026, reserve money expanded by 8.5 per cent (y-o-y) as against 5.6 per cent a year ago. Adjusted for the first-round impact of CRR change, growth in reserve money stood at 11.9 per cent (9.4 per cent a year ago). II.2 Domestic Financial Markets Money market rates softened in H1:2026-27 in tandem with evolving liquidity conditions. G-sec yields eased until August before hardening in September, reflecting higher global yields, rising oil prices, and expectations of monetary tightening. Corporate bond yields moved in sync with G-sec yields, with a hardening bias, while risk premia showed mixed trends. Equity markets gained marginally despite heightened volatility in global financial markets and crude oil prices due to West Asia conflict. The foreign exchange market remained volatile amid shifting US policies and lingering conflict in West Asia. In the credit market, both bank and non-bank credit grew at a robust pace. II.2.1 Money Market During H1:2026-27, money market rates softened and remained mostly range bound amid large surplus liquidity conditioned by robust capital inflows, especially from FCNR(B) deposits under the Reserve Bank’s swap facility announced in June 2026. The weighted average call rate (WACR) – the operating target of monetary policy – generally remained within the policy rate corridor. However, with the significant rise in surplus liquidity, it moved downward towards the SDF rate, floor of the corridor, in September ( Chart II.2a ). Volatility in the WACR, as measured by the exponential weighted moving average (EWMA) 6 , declined considerably in the beginning of FY 2026-27, however, it increased marginally in July, and remained moderate till September ( Chart II.2b ). Reflecting the evolving liquidity conditions, the average spread of WACR over the policy repo rate turned positive during May-July 2026, before turning negative in August and plunging further in September

( Chart II.2b ). Overnight rates in the collateralised segment, i.e., triparty repo (TREPS) and market repo, broadly tracked the WACR, although both fell below the SDF rate intermittently during H1:2026-27 ( Chart II.3 ). Money market activity remained concentrated in the collateralised segments (tri-party and market repo), with their share in overnight money market volume at 97 per cent. During H1:2026-27, the share of the uncollateralised segment, i.e., the call money market, persisted around 3 per cent. Mutual funds remained the major lenders in tri-party repo with their share unchanged at 65 per cent in H1:2026-27, while their share in total lending in market repo segment moderated to 41 per cent in H1 from 48 per cent in H2:2025-26. The share of foreign banks in market repo lending increased to 31 per cent in H1:2026-27 from 29 per cent in H2:2025-26. On the borrowing side, public sector banks (PSBs) were the major player in tri-party repo, with their share increasing to 35 per cent in H1:2026-27 from 32 per cent in H2:2025-26. The share of private banks reduced noticeably to 14 per cent from 24 per cent. The share of PSBs in market repo increased by 5 percentage points to 13 per cent over the same period. The rates in term segments of the money market also moved in line with the evolving liquidity conditions and uncertainty (also see Box II.1 ). While 3-month treasury bill (T-Bill) rates moved largely in line with the policy repo rate, the rates on certificates of deposits (CDs) and commercial papers (CPs) edged up in May, but moderated since July notwithstanding intermittent spikes. The average spread of CDs and CPs over the policy repo rate widened to 135 bps and 155 bps in H1:2026-27 from 116 bps and 136 bps, respectively, in H2:2025-26.

The average spread of T-Bills over the policy repo rate increased to 5 bps from 1 bp over the same period ( Chart II.3 ). Box II.1: Drivers of CD and CP Rate Spreads Rates on short-term instruments like Certificates of Deposit (CDs) and Commercial Papers (CPs) generally move in tandem with the policy repo rate but diverge at times reflecting broader liquidity conditions and funding pressures. Starting from Q3 of 2025-26, CD/CP rates hardened and remained elevated even as the monetary policy easing cycle continued. It resulted in widening of spread of CD/CP rates over the policy repo rate. Besides liquidity conditions and funding pressures, several other factors can cause CP and CD spreads to deviate from their long-run averages, including, policy uncertainty, monetary policy expectations and market-specific factors such as issuance patterns, calendar effects, and episodes of market stress (Priyadarshini et al., 2024, Anshul et al., 2025). To disentangle the respective contribution of various factors which are intertwined and may operate simultaneously, uncorrelated shocks are identified using historical decompositions within a VAR framework using monthly data. The following VAR specification is used. Where Y t includes the selected endogenous variables, X t contains the exogenous dummies and Pε t are the orthogonalised shocks. The variables are selected to capture the main channels, viz., banking system liquidity, funding conditions and policy uncertainty through which they can affect short-term funding costs, while avoiding overlap across closely related measures. 7 For CDs, the funding block also captures banks’ balance-sheet pressures through changes in outstanding credit-deposit ratio and net CD issuance growth. For CPs, only net issuance growth is used to capture funding conditions. The uncorrelated shocks are identified using a recursive identification scheme where the most exogenous factors are placed at the top while the response variable, i.e., CD or CP

spreads are placed at the end of the ordering. Historical decomposition for the period January 2025 – July 2026 show the extent of contribution by each identified factor to the movements in spreads ( Chart II.1.1 ). The decomposition results suggest that the drivers of CD and CP spreads have shifted over time. Relatively tight liquidity conditions were the main driver of widening spreads during early 2025, but increased system liquidity along with policy rate easing led spreads to moderate to relatively lower levels by mid-2025. Since late 2025, the spreads hardened again. Funding pressures, owing to stronger credit growth relative to deposit mobilisation, contributed to hardening of CD spread, while economic policy uncertainty was the main driver of widening CP spread. More recently, idiosyncratic market-specific pressures have also contributed to the widening which are unrelated to the identified shocks in the model. II.2.3 Corporate Bond Market Corporate bond yields evolved in sync with G-sec yields with a hardening bias during H1:2026-27, while the risk premia showed mixed trends ( Chart II.10a ). The average bond market risk premium (i.e., the spread of 3-year AAA corporate bond yields over 3-year G-sec yields) hardened from 129 bps to 140 bps for NBFCs, and from 112 bps to 122 bps for corporates, but remained stable at 109 bps for Public Sector Units (PSUs), Financial Institutions (FIs) and banks in H1, even as corporate earnings remained robust in Q1 ( Chart II.10b and Table II.4 ). Primary issuances of listed corporate bonds in domestic markets declined by 17.9 per cent during H1:2026-27 (up to August 2026) as compared to the corresponding period of the previous year reflecting higher yields ( Chart II.11a ). Overseas issuances increased to ₹1,31,931 crore during H1:2026-27 (up to August 2026) from ₹10,303 crore during the same period last year, partly attributed to RBI’s swap facility. Most of the resource mobilisation in the corporate bond market (99 per cent) was through the private placement route. Outstanding investments by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) in corporate bonds stood at ₹2.7 lakh crore as at end-September, 2026 with utilisation of investment limits at 29.3 per cent ( Chart II.11b ). Trading volume in the secondary market moderated to ₹9.5 lakh crore during H1 (up to August 2026) from ₹10.1 lakh crore during the corresponding period of the previous year. II.2.4 Equity Market During H1:2026-27, Indian equity markets gained despite heightened volatility in global financial markets and crude oil prices due to conflict in West Asia. Markets rebounded in April 2026

following the announcement of the US-Iran ceasefire. However, equity market remained subdued in May and early June as persistent tensions in West Asia, elevated crude oil prices and the IMD’s forecast of below normal monsoon weighed on investor sentiment. Thereafter, markets gained reflecting resilient corporate earnings results and a rebound in net buying by FPIs, even as the disruption of the US-Iran ceasefire reversed some gains in early July. Equity prices declined towards the end of August and early September amidst lingering geopolitical uncertainties, rising crude oil prices and higher global bond yields. II.2.5 Foreign Exchange Market The foreign exchange market remained volatile during H1:2026-27, driven by shifting US policies on tariff and policy rate, and lingering conflict in West Asia. While the rupee initially depreciated in the aftermath of the West Asia conflict, policy measures announced by the Reserve Bank and the Government to bolster capital flows arrested its decline. The implied volatility cooled down after peaking to a multi-year high in the wake of the West Asia conflict ( Chart II.15 ). Overall, the rupee depreciated by 1.4 per cent against the US dollar in H1:2026-27, a marked moderation from the sharp depreciation of 6.2 per cent witnessed in H2:2025-26 ( Chart II.16 ). The relative standing of the rupee among EM currencies also improved even as the pressures from volatile global market, elevated crude oil prices and the prolonged West Asia conflict weighed on the currency. Forward premia moderated during H1:2026-27 from the peak seen in the first week of April, supported by measures undertaken by the Government and the Reserve Bank to attract foreign capital. Upward pressures persisted, however, reflecting volatility in crude oil prices and flare-up of tensions in West Asia conflict ( Chart II.17 ). In terms of the 40-currency real effective exchange rate (REER), the INR depreciated by 0.5 per cent between March and August 2026, driven by the depreciation of the rupee in nominal terms ( Chart II.18a ).

During the period, the movement in REER index was modest, as compared to major peer emerging economies ( Chart II.18b ). II.2.6 Bank and Non-Bank Credit Bank Credit: Aggregate Trends Bank credit growth strengthened further during H1: 2026–27 (up to September 15), on the back of robust loan demand ( Chart II.19 ). As on September 15, 2026, credit growth (y-o-y) for scheduled commercial banks (SCBs) accelerated sharply to 18.1 per cent, from 10.4 per cent during the corresponding period in the previous year ( Chart II.20 ). Across bank groups, foreign banks recorded the highest credit expansion at 25.8 per cent y-o-y, outperforming private banks (PVBs) at 19.1 per cent and public sector banks (PSBs) at 16.9 per cent. While PSBs contributed the largest share to y-o-y incremental credit, their overall market share contracted due to aggressive lending by both PVBs and foreign banks. The asset quality of SCBs strengthened further in Q1:2026-27 with the overall gross non-performing assets (NPA) ratio declining to 1.8 per cent in June 2026 from 2.3 per cent a year ago ( Chart II.21a ). The improvement spanned all major sectors, except for services and retail loans, where asset quality remained unchanged ( Chart II.21b ). Banks’ non statutory liquidity ratio (non-SLR) investments (comprising CPs, bonds, debentures, and shares of public and private corporates) increased by around 2.9 per cent during H1:2026-27 (up to September 15), with an increase in investments in commercial papers due to higher returns ( Chart II.22a ). Growth in adjusted non-food bank credit (i.e., non-food bank credit plus banks’ non-SLR investments) accelerated to 17.6 per cent (y-o-y) in Q2:2026-27 (up to September 15) from 10.1 per cent in Q2:2025-26, ( Chart II.22b ). As on August 31, 2026, excess holdings of SLR securities by SCBs marginally moderated to 6.3

per cent of their net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) from 6.4 per cent at end-March 2026 as banks brought down their investment portfolio to fund credit demand ( Chart II.23 ). Bank Credit: A Sectoral Perspective Sectoral trends 8 , 9 indicate strengthening of credit growth across major segments. Sustained robust economic activity continued to underpin credit demand, supporting broad-based expansion in bank credit. Monetary policy was found to have heterogenous impact on sectoral credit growth ( Box II.2 ). Box II.2: Bank Lending Channel of Monetary Policy: A Sectoral Approach Indian financial system continues to be bank-dominated. Bank credit as a proportion to GDP surged from 52.8 per cent in 2011-12 to 59.8 per cent in 2025-26. Therefore, given the importance of the banking sector, it becomes pertinent to understand the effectiveness of the transmission of monetary policy through the lending channel to various sectors of the economy. Under the current policy easing cycle, bank credit has inched up considerably across sectors. Demand conditions for credit have also been strong on the back of persisting buoyancy in domestic economic activity. In this milieu, it would be important to empirically decipher the response of sectoral bank credit to monetary policy shocks. Against this backdrop, the dynamic response of overall bank credit and credit to major sectors over 24 months following an unexpected policy rate change is examined using panel local projection technique (Jordà, 2005). Policy surprises are extracted using data on Overnight Index Swap (OIS) rates around RBI policy announcement dates, after controlling for current macroeconomic conditions (Lakdawala and Sengupta, 2025). Using monthly bank-level panel data of 40 banks for the period March 2014 - March 2026, the baseline specification for each horizon h = 0, 1, ..., 24 is given as under: Where, y i,t represents credit growth

for bank i in time t, y i,t+h – y i,t–1 is the dependent variable representing the cumulative credit growth for bank i from the pre-shock period to horizon h, α i,h are bank fixed effects at horizon h, Shock t is the exogenous monetary policy (target factor) shock at time t, and β h is the coefficient of interest, capturing the cumulative impulse response of bank credit to a one standard deviation monetary policy shock at horizon h. Plotting β h for h = 0, 1, ..., 24 traces the impulse response function. Shock t–j are lagged shocks controlling for prior monetary policy actions, Δy i,t–j controls for lagged values of the dependent variable, credit growth, X i,t–1 is a vector of lagged bank characteristics (size, soundness, profitability, credit to deposits and borrowing ratio and asset quality) that can affect credit growth, MC t–p are lagged macroeconomic controls (nominal GDP growth and inflation) and D t and C t are dummies for demonetisation and COVID-19 pandemic, respectively. ε i,t+h is the idiosyncratic error term clustered at the bank level. The lag length (p) is set to 12 months following the documented 6-to-18-month transmission lag in the Indian banking sector (Khundrakpam and Jain, 2012; Raj, et al, 2020). The impulse response of aggregate non-food credit to a one standard deviation expansionary monetary policy shock indicates that credit expands over the short to medium term, increasing by approximately 0.50 percentage points (pp) within the first six months, peaking to 0.8 pp around 13 months after the shock but becomes insignificant by the 15th month. Credit growth increases immediately following expansionary monetary policy shocks, reaches a peak after one year, and gradually reverts as balance sheets adjust ( Chart II.2.1 ). Across major sectors, the impact of the expansionary monetary policy shock

is found to be heterogeneous. Credit to agriculture sector remains steady initially, before expanding from around 4th month onwards, reaching the peak in around 18 months. Industry and services sectors respond immediately to the monetary policy shock, with industry reaching its peak expansion earlier (around 10 months) than services (around 13 months), after which both sectors’ responses gradually taper off. The response of personal loans is found to be delayed, remaining flat over the first few months, but it follows a steeper expansion and peaks around 10th month, like industry ( Chart II.2.2 ). Industrial credit growth also picked up and it was above its compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) over the last 10-year period in H1:2026-27, supporting overall credit expansion ( Table II.5 ). Services and personal loans continued to drive overall credit growth ( Chart II.24 ). Credit to industrial sector registered robust growth during H1:2026-27, largely attributable to a sharp

acceleration in credit to large industries. This was supported partly by corporates’ reduced recourse to market-based funding as its cost was higher on account of heightened geopolitical tensions. Credit to MSMEs 10 continued on its double-digit growth trajectory, reflecting resilient credit demand including increased working capital requirements amidst global uncertainties and continued policy support. The policy support measures comprise the enhanced guarantee limit under the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) scheme, Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) 5.0, among others ( Chart II.25 ). Among the major industrial sub-sectors, credit growth in infrastructure segment made a significant contribution to overall industrial credit expansion. 'Basic metal and metal products', ‘all engineering’ and 'chemicals and chemical products' also aided industrial growth ( Chart II.25b ). Within services sector, 'non-banking financial companies' (NBFCs) remained the largest recipient of bank credit during H1:2026-27, with improved availability following the withdrawal of the additional risk-weights effective April 1, 2025. Credit to services excluding NBFCs also expanded at a steady pace. Segments, such as trade and commercial real estate, recorded robust growth ( Chart II.26 ). Credit growth in personal loans segment remained buoyant during H1:2026-27, driven primarily by housing, loans against gold jewellery and vehicle loans. Housing loans, which account for nearly half of the personal loans, continued to grow at a steady pace reflecting robust real estate activity. Growth in loans against gold jewellery, albeit moderating from its peak in June 2025, remained elevated, which may be attributed to higher gold prices resulting in increased collateral valuation along with revised regulations effective from April 1, 2026 11 . Vehicle loan growth accelerated sharply, nearly doubling vis-à-vis the previous year, on the back of persistent demand following the GST cut ( Chart II.27 ). NBFC Credit: A Sectoral Perspective 12 Credit

extended by NBFCs exhibited robust expansion since August 2025, driven primarily by strong retail credit. The marked acceleration in credit growth to segments such as housing and gold, coupled with steady credit expansion in vehicle loans, drove the buoyant expansion in retail credit. Industrial credit growth softened, reflecting a moderation in lending to infrastructure, especially power sector, during H1:2026-27 (up to August). Credit growth in services sector remain strong despite some deceleration in recent months vis-à-vis last year ( Table II.6 ). The continued buoyancy in retail lending underscored NBFCs' role in complementing the banking sector by catering to credit requirements of a diverse range of borrowers. At the same time, the weighted average lending rate (WALR) of banks have firmed up for fresh rupee loans, owing to strong credit demand. Bank credit growth outpaced deposit growth, leading to increased funding pressure. During H1 (till August), the WALR on fresh rupee loans increased by 21 bps, while it declined modestly by 3 bps for outstanding loans. In response to a cumulative reduction of 125 bps in the policy repo rate during February 2025 to August 2026, the WADTDRs for fresh and outstanding deposits have declined by 95 bps and 53 bps, respectively. On the lending side, WALRs for fresh and outstanding loans have declined by 72 bps and 91 bps, respectively. The share of the external benchmark-based lending rate (EBLR) linked loans in total outstanding floating rate loans of scheduled commercial banks increased from 67.6 per cent as at end-March 2026 to 68.2 per cent at end-June 2026. Consequently, the share of MCLR-linked loans declined from 30.2 per cent to 29.6 per cent. Public sector banks (PSBs) still have a significant proportion of their loans linked to MCLR ( Chart II.28a ),

while private banks (PVBs) extend a large part of their loans at EBLR ( Chart II.28b ). The MCLR and other legacy rates – based on internal benchmarks and with longer reset periods – act as an impediment to faster policy transmission. PSBs have a high share of MCLR-linked loans in agriculture, infrastructure, other personal loans and large industry ( Chart II.29a ). The shares of MCLR-linked loans are lower for PVBs than those in PSBs ( Chart II.29b ). Bank group-wise, the transmission to WALRs on fresh and outstanding rupee loans of PVBs was higher than that of PSBs ( Chart II.30a ). The large share of EBLR-linked loans may have facilitated higher transmission in case of PVBs compared to PSBs. However, lending rates of PVBs remained above those of PSBs ( Chart II.30b ). The maximum pass-through to lending rates was witnessed among foreign banks, reflecting their higher share of EBLR-linked loans 13 and a higher share of low-cost bulk deposits of lower maturity. Sectoral analysis shows that the transmission to lending rates has been heterogeneous due to varying proportions of credit portfolios linked to fixed and floating interest rates and differential spreads charged by banks. Furthermore, the shifts in volumes across banks/sectors towards higher/lower interest rate slabs could impact aggregate lending rates. The WALRs showed a broad based decline across sectors since February 2025. The volume effect, however, partially dampened transmission in other personal loans and trade in fresh loans, whereas it complemented in sectors such as agriculture and education, thereby enhancing transmission ( Chart II.31 ). For EBLR-linked loans, PVBs have increased their spreads (charged over the repo rate) for education, housing, MSMEs and vehicle loans, which dampened the extent of transmission ( Table II.8 ). On the other hand, PSBs have reduced spread in education,

MSME and vehicle loans, and increased it in other personal loans. For domestic banks, spread was higher in August 2026 over January 2025 for all sectors except education and vehicle loans. Through their extensive outreach and specialised lending activities across sectors, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) substantially contribute to the transmission of monetary policy via the credit channel. Nevertheless, NBFCs typically charge higher lending rates compared to SCBs, mainly due to differences in the risk profile of borrowers, their funding structures, and cost of liabilities. During February 2025 to August 2026, lending rates of NBFCs moderated across sectors. The highest transmission in fresh lending rates was recorded in advances against gold followed by vehicle and MSME loans ( Chart II.32 ). The Government of India reviewed the interest rates on various small savings instruments, which are linked to secondary market yields on G-secs of comparable maturities, and kept them unchanged for Q3:2026-27, marking 11 consecutive quarters with no change in rates. This has led to substantial positive spread of small saving instrument rates over their formula-based rates except for public provident fund ( Table II.9 ). The widening gaps may be limiting the transmission of policy rates to banks’ deposit rates,

especially during policy easing, because of the potential substitution effect. A large interest rate differential in favour of small savings could lead to migration of deposits away from banks, thus widening the credit-deposit gap in the banking system. II.4 Conclusion Financial markets conditions remained largely congenial during H1:2026-27, with intermittent bouts of volatility arising from geopolitical uncertainties, fluctuations in crude oil prices and capital flows. System liquidity remained in surplus for most of the period, aided by capital inflows under the Reserve Bank’s special swap facilities. Money market rates softened and remained largely range bound in line with the evolving liquidity conditions. Government bond yields softened before hardening in September, mainly reflecting global developments. Corporate bond yields moved in tandem with G-sec yields. Domestic equity markets gained in H1, supported by robust corporate earnings, and renewed buying by foreign investors. The Indian rupee experienced two-way movements with a depreciating bias, although the pace of depreciation moderated. Bank credit growth remained robust and broad-based across major sectors. The non-bank sources of finance also expanded. Transmission to deposit rates further strengthened in H1, while it moderated in the case of lending rates. Going ahead, liquidity management operations will be conditional on evolving domestic financial conditions, monetary policy decisions and the stance of monetary policy.
