III. Demand and Output Domestic economic activity exhibited resilience in H1:2026-27, despite continued global uncertainty. Real GDP posted a strong growth of 7.8 per cent in Q1:2026-27. Private final consumption remained healthy, supported by buoyant discretionary consumption. Revival in private capex and government’s continued focus on infrastructure spending strengthened investment activity. Manufacturing expanded at a robust pace, while services sector maintained its buoyancy. Looking ahead, weak monsoons, the prolonged West-Asia conflict, additional frictions in global trade and tighter global financial conditions may have an adverse bearing on both the demand and supply side of the economy. Domestic economic activity exhibited resilience in H1:2026-27, despite continued global uncertainty amidst the prolonged West-Asia conflict. The supply-side pressures were effectively dealt with proactive policy measures that ensured supply of key inputs for productive sectors. As per the National Statistics Office (NSO)’s estimates, real GDP recorded a growth of 7.8 per cent in Q1:2026-27 reflecting strong momentum in underlying economic activity. Aggregate demand remained strong on the back of both private consumption and investment. Net external demand also contributed positively to growth with rebound in merchandise exports and sustained buoyancy in services exports. On the supply side, both manufacturing and services sectors recorded strong growth in Q1. Going ahead, weak monsoon and El Niño may weigh on agricultural activity. Industry and services sectors are expected to continue benefitting from the

Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme 5.0 and the Transition Facilitation (Quality Control) Order 2026. Similarly, India’s growing network of bilateral free trade agreements (FTAs) augurs well for external demand, though uncertainties about additional tariffs on US imports, including those under Section 301, pose some risk. The risks from protracted West Asia conflict and financial market repricing due to changes in US monetary policy also require close monitoring. III.1 Aggregate Demand Aggregate demand conditions in the economy held up well in Q1:2026-27. As per the statistics released by the National Statistics Office, real GDP grew by 7.8 per cent, up from 6.9 per cent a year ago. Despite modest rise in domestic prices of select commodities, private final consumption expenditure (PFCE) remained healthy, while double-digit growth in gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) suggests a strong recovery in the capex cycle ( Table III.1 ). Private final consumption contributed almost half of GDP growth in Q1:2026-27, though lower than 54.6 per cent a year ago. Strong growth in gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) also led to a sharp rise in its contribution to growth. By contrast, the contribution of government final consumption expenditure moderated in Q1. As real imports contracted and real exports rose sharply, net external demand was a positive contributor to GDP growth for the second successive quarter in Q1 ( Table III.1 and Chart III.1a ). The momentum of GDP – quarter-on-quarter (q-o-q) seasonally adjusted annualised growth rate (SAAR) – was placed at 6.5 per cent in Q1 ( Chart III.1b ). III.1.1 Private Final Consumption Expenditure Private consumption growth in Q1:2026-27 remained strong at 7.1 per cent compared to 6.8 per cent during the same quarter last year, supported by buoyant discretionary spending. The rising purchasing power of households, buoyed by a prolonged phase of low inflation, stable employment conditions, tax rationalisation, and robust rabi production in previous quarters bolstered households' discretionary spending. Among major high frequency indicators, passenger vehicle sales recorded double-digit growth in April-July 2026. Demand for consumer durables increased at a healthy pace in Q1 and July-August, while growth in consumer non-durables remained subdued. The non-housing retail loans, which generally support discretionary spending, also increased at a robust pace. Slowdown in domestic air passenger traffic since February 2026 reflected price pressures amid the West Asia conflict. Tractor sales expanded at a robust pace during April-July, before remaining flat in August, which coupled with buoyant growth in two-wheeler sales during April-August, imply strong rural

demand conditions. However, the increase in demand for work under the Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) [earlier MGNREGA] in August- September 2026 due to weakening of agricultural activity reflects a shift of rural households towards low-paying jobs ( Table III.2 ). The extent of pass-through of input costs, impact of weak monsoon on rural income, and continued momentum in manufacturing and service sector activities will remain pivotal to the sustenance of overall PFCE growth. Government’s policy measures to support agriculture, resilient agriculture allied sectors, and a wider fiscal safety net through direct benefit transfers may help protect rural income and consumption. III.1.3 Government Consumption Government final consumption expenditure (GFCE) in real terms grew by 4.3 per cent (y-o-y) in Q1:2026-27 compared to 7.7 per cent in the previous quarter ( Table III.1 ). On the expenditure front, revenue expenditure of the central government (excluding interest payments and major subsidies) registered a growth of 12.5 per cent during April-August 2026 on a y-o-y basis, as compared to marginal contraction of 0.3 per cent during the same period of the last fiscal year ( Chart III.5a ). Expenditure on major subsidies (comprising food, fertiliser, and petroleum) of the Centre registered a double-digit growth of 24.4 per cent during April-August 2026 3 led by expansion in fertiliser and food subsidy. Interest payments by the Centre, however, contracted during April-August 2026, over the corresponding period of 2025-26. Capital expenditure of the Centre registered a y-o-y growth of 18.2 per cent during April-August 2026 ( Chart III.5a ). Accordingly, the quality of government expenditure improved as the ratio of revenue expenditure to capital outlay (RECO) declined in April-August 2026, boding well for infrastructure-led development 4 ( Chart III.5b ). Amidst the ongoing West Asia crisis and lingering trade policy uncertainty, global demand conditions continue to remain fragile. Strong demand for AI-related goods and the frontloading of consumer goods in anticipation of additional US tariffs after the expiration of temporary tariffs in July 2026 9 , however, supported international trade. India's merchandise exports also rebounded and grew by 17.8 per cent in H1:2026-27 (April-August). With merchandise imports growing at a higher pace than exports, the merchandise trade deficit expanded to US$147.1 billion in H1:2026-27 (April-August) from US$ 123.9 billion in H1:2025-26 (April-August) ( Chart III.10 ). Improvement in export performance was broad-based as the share of commodity groups with double-digit growth in H1:2026-27 (April-August) was 73.4 per cent vis-à-vis 16.2 per cent in H1:2025-26 (April-August). Petroleum products; engineering goods; electronic goods; organic and inorganic chemicals; and meat, dairy and poultry products were the main drivers of merchandise exports growth. Exports to the US remained resilient, primarily driven by electronic goods and engineering goods. Sectors that were a drag on exports included readymade garments of all textiles; ceramic products and glassware; fruits and vegetables; tobacco; and spices ( Chart III.11a and b ). The growth in merchandise imports during H1:2026-27 (April-August) was driven by higher imports of electronic goods; petroleum, crude and products; machinery, electrical and non-electrical; fertilisers, crude and manufactured; and non-ferrous metals. By contrast, chemical material and products; pearls, precious and semi-precious stones; iron and steel; silver; and pulp and waste paper contributed negatively to import growth ( Chart III.12 ). Gold imports at US$ 17.5 billion grew by 3.4 per cent during this period, while petroleum, crude and products imports grew by 22.4 per cent to US$ 95.6 billion, both reflecting the value impact due to steep rise in prices. Despite elevated trade uncertainty, both net terms of

trade and income terms of trade improved in Q1:2026-27 vis-à-vis Q4: 2025-26, implying greater purchasing power of exports in terms of imports. As prices of key imports softened in June, net terms of trade in Q1 recouped from losses in the previous quarter ( Chart III.13 ). India’s services exports growth remained robust at 10.9 per cent (y-o-y) in April-August 2026, led by software and business services ( Chart III.14 ). India remains one of the top five service-exporting countries worldwide in terms of export growth in Q1:2026-27. Services imports also registered a strong growth in April-August 2026 on the back of higher transport and business services. Net services surplus increased by 7.3 per cent to US$ 85.8 billion in April-August 2026. Despite significant widening of the goods trade deficit, the current account deficit (CAD) at US$ 4.2 billion (0.5 per cent of GDP) in Q1:2026-27 was marginally higher than its level of US$ 3.4 billion (0.4 per cent of GDP) in Q1:2025-26 ( Chart III.15 ). Services and remittance receipts continued to support the current account. There were net capital outflows of US$ 3.9 billion in Q1, as against net inflows of US$ 7.9 billion last year. 10 Consequently, India’s foreign exchange reserves depleted by US$ 8.1 billion (BoP basis) during the quarter. As per preliminary estimates, CAD widened to US$ 7.0 billion in July 2026 from US$ 3.2 billion a year ago, driven by higher merchandise trade deficit and net income outgoes. India’s gross inward foreign direct investment (FDI) and net FDI flows were higher in April-August 2026, both on y-o-y as well as sequential basis. A slowdown in the pace of outward FDI along with sustained higher gross FDI inflows supported net FDI flows. Financial services, communication services, computer services and manufacturing accounted for around 73 per

cent of total FDI equity inflows during April-August 2026. In terms of origin, Singapore, Japan, Mauritius, The United Arab Emirates and the US were major sources of inward FDI to India, accounting for around 81 per cent of total inflows. Foreign portfolio investment (FPI) registered net outflows of US$ 8.9 billion during 2026-27 (up to September). After recording sustained outflows during the first quarter following geopolitical tensions in Middle East, FPI turned positive during June-August 2026 supported by measures taken by the RBI and the Government ( Table III.8 ). FPI flows reversed again in September 2026 amidst rising global risk-off sentiment on re-escalation of Middle East tensions and rising US bond yields. External commercial borrowing (ECB) agreements during April-August 2026 (P) increased significantly by 93.4 per cent (y-o-y) to US$ 30.4 billion, partly attributed to the RBI’s concessional US dollar-rupee swap facility introduced in June 2026 11 . Consequently, net ECB inflows to India 12 grew by 55.9 per cent to US$ 7.3 billion during April-August 2026 from US$ 4.7 billion a year ago. In terms of utilisation, on-lending/ sub-lending accounted for the highest share (28.0 per cent), followed by general corporate purpose (13.8 per cent) and refinancing of rupee loans (11.9 per cent) during this period. As at end-August 2026, about 73.0 per cent of outstanding ECBs (excluding rupee and inter-company borrowings) were hedged by the Indian companies. Net inflows under non-resident deposits stood at US$ 119.2 billion during April-August 2026 (P), significantly higher than US$ 5.6 billion a year ago due to a surge in FCNR(B) deposits on account of RBI’s forex swap facility. During June 8 - August 31, 2026, gross inflows under the FCNR(B) deposit scheme stood at US$ 133.0 billion 13 . As of September 25, 2026, India’s foreign exchange reserves stood at US$

747.6 billion which is equivalent to 10.9 months of goods imports and 96.1 per cent of the external debt outstanding as at end-June 2026. III.2.1 Agriculture Real GVA in agriculture and allied activities grew by 3.6 per cent in Q1:2026-27, lower than a year earlier. Robust growth in allied activities supported the overall growth in this sector. The shortfall and regional unevenness of Southwest monsoon and El Niño effects may pose some risks to both kharif and rabi output, though non-farm rural activities have shown greater resilience in recent years ( Box III.1 ). The Southwest monsoon, after remaining weak in June, gained significant momentum subsequently, covering the entire country by July 9, 2026. Monsoon remained 1.0 per cent above the long period average (LPA) in July and supported kharif sowing. As of September 30, 2026, the cumulative rainfall was 12.6 per cent below the Long Period Average ( Chart III.17a ). In terms of spatial distribution, rainfall remained deficient compared to the LPA across all regions. As of September 30, 2026, the production-weighted rainfall index (PRN) stood at 90 per cent, suggesting a skewed rainfall distribution in major crop producing states ( Chart III.17b ). As of October 1, 2026, reservoir levels at 71.8 per cent remained below normal

level 14 (81.8 per cent) and last year’s level (90.3 per cent), due to erratic monsoon ( Chart III.17c ). Box III.1: Indian Agricultural Sector amidst Weather Shocks Rainfall shortfalls remain a major driver of year-to-year fluctuation in agricultural output. However, the rural economy is increasingly cushioned from erratic monsoon by resilient allied sector activities. Chand and Singh (2026) observe that for agricultural households possessing land up to one acre, wages contribute more than 55 per cent of household income, while crop production and livestock together contribute 36 per cent. This suggests that rural household incomes are increasingly supported by activities beyond crop production. Although annual estimates of value added are not available separately for rural and urban areas, historical benchmark estimates support the use of a broad rural-linked proxy. In 1999-2000, agriculture, forestry and fishing, mining and quarrying, and construction together accounted for about 59 per cent of total rural net domestic product (Central Statistical Organisation, 2007). This exercise therefore uses the sum of GVA of these sectors as an indicative proxy for rural-linked activity. Data available for both base years (i.e., 2011-12 and 2022-23) suggest that the non-agricultural component has become more important over time ( Chart III.1.1 ). The growth-rate analysis below is calculated within the relevant published GVA base, with 2023-24 onward using the 2022-23-base series. Rainfall sensitivity differs across the two components of the proxy, viz., agricultural and non-agricultural ( Chart III.1.2a ). Agricultural growth suffers more in years of higher monsoon deficit, while growth in the non-agricultural component stays close to 6 per cent at every cut-off. In years of surplus rainfall, by contrast, agricultural growth averages 5.1 per cent, above the 4.3 per cent recorded in years close to the LPA. It is estimated that non-agricultural activity was the predominant contributor to growth

in rural economic activity during years of rainfall deficiency exceeding 7 per cent, as against in other years. The same contrast is evident in the regression estimates ( Chart III.1.2b ). Over 1994-95 to 2025-26, a regression of annual growth of agriculture and allied activities on the rainfall shortfall from the long-period average gives a coefficient of (–) 0.40, statistically significant at 1 per cent. The shortfall measure explains about 39 per cent of the variation in agricultural growth. For the non-agricultural component, the coefficient is 0.01 but not statistically significant ( Chart III.1.2b ). The pattern is also stable across two equal sub-periods. Including a separate term for rainfall above the LPA leaves the shortfall coefficient for agriculture largely unchanged at (–)0.44, while the excess-rainfall term is small and not statistically significant at (–)0.12. A formal test rejects a symmetric response to deficient and surplus rainfall for agriculture (p value = 0.04) but not for the non-agricultural component. The asymmetry is not an artefact of the censoring implicit in the shortfall measure. The evidence on the declining role of rainfall in crop production is in line with Gupta et al. 2023. The factors that seem to have reduced the sensitivity of agricultural activity to rainfall shortfall include increased irrigation coverage, new weather resilient crop varieties, and diversification towards less water-intensive crops. At the same time, the composition of agricultural output has shifted towards allied activities. Over 1999-2000 to 2024-25, the coefficient for agriculture and allied GVA is (–)0.44 and significant at 1 per cent while the coefficients for milk, eggs, meat and fish as well as non-agricultural component are small and statistically insignificant ( Chart III.1.3a ). These estimates suggest that growth in these activities is less closely related to aggregate rainfall shortfalls than agricultural GVA. Rolling correlations of

the absolute deviation of rainfall from the LPA with growth in agricultural GVA and the rural-linked activity proxy have generally become less negative since the mid-2000s (irrespective of the window-length), while remaining below zero throughout ( Charts III.1.3b ). Summing up, empirical findings suggest that while rainfall shortfalls remain important for agricultural output, their association with allied activities and other rural-linked activity has moderated over time. Diversification across rural-linked activity and within agriculture has made the rural economy more resilient to rainfall shortfall. References: Chand, R., and J. III.3 Conclusion Strong real GDP growth in Q1:2026-27, amidst global uncertainty and supply-side disruptions, signifies the inherent strength of the economy on the back of sustained focus on structural reforms, proactive policy responses, resilient macroeconomic fundamentals, and buoyant domestic demand. High frequency indicators available for Q2 suggest continued buoyancy in domestic economic activity, albeit with some moderation compared to Q1. Stable employment conditions, continued positive impact of tax rationalisation, congenial financial conditions, revival in corporate investment, and a pickup in goods exports are expected to support economic activity going forward. While a double-digit growth in GFCF reflects improving investment sentiment, sustenance of private consumption growth will be vital to broad-based recovery in private capex. Going forward, weak monsoons coupled with strong El Niño,

IV. Prices and Costs Headline CPI inflation increased sequentially, rising above the target during June-August driven by a sustained positive price momentum. Higher food and fuel inflation led to this increase, reflecting adverse weather conditions and the sharp rise in energy prices following the West Asia conflict. Core inflation registered a pick-up with signs of generalisation in recent months. Going ahead, persistent supply-side pressures in food and volatile global energy prices pose risks to the domestic inflation outlook, particularly through second-round effects amid strong growth impulses. IV.1 Introduction The headline consumer price index (CPI) inflation 1 has been increasing steadily in the period since the release of the previous MPR in April 2026. From 3.4 per cent in March 2026, headline inflation increased over successive months to 4.4 per cent in June (the first print above the inflation target in seventeen months) and further to 4.8 per cent in August ( Chart IV.1a ). The sequential pick-up in inflation witnessed since March was driven by a strong price momentum, which more than offset the favourable base effects in each month ( Chart IV.1b ). 2 The momentum has been particularly strong since May. Among the major sub-components, food and fuel

recorded sharp increases in y-o-y inflation over March levels ( Chart IV.2a ). Reflecting this, the contribution of food and fuel sub-components to headline inflation increased significantly ( Chart IV.2b ). The pick-up in food inflation was driven by unfavourable weather conditions and increasing fuel prices brought about by the sharp upturn in global energy prices following the West Asia conflict. Core inflation (CPI excluding food and fuel) also registered a pick-up, albeit by a lower magnitude upto July, reflecting limited pass-through of supply side pressures. In August core inflation accelerated to 4.2 per cent. The April MPR projections had factored in risks from the West Asia conflict and adverse weather conditions as part of the baseline forecast. Reflecting this, the actual inflation outcomes remained broadly in line with the projections ( Chart IV.3 ). 3 Inflation for Q2:2026-27 so far (July-August) has turned out to be about 20 basis points (bps) higher than the quarterly average projection, as food price pressures have accentuated in recent months. The remainder of the chapter delves deeper into component-wise developments in inflation, statistical properties of observed inflation trends as well as determinants of inflation. IV.2 Developments across Major Components of the CPI CPI Food and Beverages Food and beverages inflation increased from 3.7 per cent in March to 5.7 per cent in August 2026, driven by items other than vegetables ( Chart IV.4 ). Of the 200-bps increase in food inflation in August over March, nearly 48 per cent was contributed by two sub-components, viz., animal protein 4 and spices 5 , which together have a weight of about 36 per cent within the food and beverages division. The increase in inflation in animal protein primarily reflected rising input costs ( Chart IV.5a ). Higher feed and fodder costs, high transportation and packaging

outlays, elevated energy prices, and heatwave-induced bird mortality contributed to the firming up of prices ( Chart IV.5b ). Inflation in spices rose steadily since January 2026 and touched 13.0 per cent in August, after being in deflation for a prolonged period. 6 Ginger, dry chillies and coriander contributed the most to the increase. The emergence of El Niño conditions and deficient southwest monsoon have raised risks to overall food price outlook. However, robust domestic production in the previous year, comfortable foodgrain stocks 7 , conducive trade policy measures and proactive supply management provided some cushion, keeping the cumulative price build-up so far broadly in line with that of non-El Niño years ( Chart IV.6 ). Among the major products, inflation in cereals and products 8 increased to 2.8 per cent in August 2026 from -0.2 per cent in April amidst a pickup in rice prices on account of lower kharif sowing ( Chart IV.7a ). The build-up in cereals prices during 2026-27 (up to August) has also been above the historical average ( Chart IV.7b ). Pulses 9 recorded a modest increase in y-o-y inflation, largely reflecting unfavourable base effects after remaining in deflation through most of 2025-26. Imports of key pulses from Myanmar, Brazil and Australia, along with government interventions in retail markets, helped keep prices at moderate levels. 10 Inflation in oils and fats was lower at 7.8 per cent by August 2026 as compared to over 20 per cent a year ago ( Chart IV.8a ). Despite the moderation, elevated global edible oil prices amid increased diversion towards biofuel production in major producing economies continue to pose pressure on domestic prices. Domestically, tighter mustard seed arrivals amid steady export demand also kept mustard oil prices elevated ( Chart IV.8b ). However, reduction in basic import duty

on crude palm, soybean and sunflower oils is likely to soften domestic prices. 11 Vegetables 12 inflation remained moderate, averaging 3.5 per cent (y-o-y) in H1:2026-27 so far (April-August 2026), supported by improved production and robust market arrivals. 13 The price build-up in the Tomato, Onion and Potato (TOP) category was broadly aligned with its historical seasonal pattern while the increase in non-TOP vegetable prices remained below that observed in both El Niño and non-El Niño years ( Chart IV.9 ). The impact of the deficient 14 and uneven spatial rainfall distribution and lower kharif sowing 15 on food prices is reflected in the recent high frequency retail price data in certain food items such as sugar and onion. Sugar 16 prices increased by about 34 per cent since the first week of July to reach ₹65/ kg by late August, due to lower than anticipated domestic production, lower carry-over stocks, and precautionary stocking by market intermediaries 17 ( Chart IV.10 ). The government undertook targeted measures such as export restrictions, stock limits on dealers and bulk consumers, duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar, physical verification of stocks, and advancing the sugarcane crushing season to augment domestic availability and contain speculative pressures. Prices have since retreated in September. Onion prices have increased by about 84 per cent since end-June (up to September 30) due to depletion/ some spoilage of stored rabi stocks and concerns over the timing and quality of kharif arrivals amid uneven rainfall ( Chart IV.11 ). Although onion prices exhibit a seasonal uptick during August-September before the arrival of the kharif crops, the magnitude of increase has been much higher this year than the historical average. CPI Fuel Global crude oil prices ratcheted up since March 2026 along with an increase in

the premium for refined products on account of extreme market tightness ( Chart IV.12 ). Reflecting the partial pass-through of this increase, CPI fuel 18 inflation went up from 0.4 per cent in April to 5.2 per cent in August. Among household fuel items included in CPI, domestic liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices were revised upwards by ₹60 per cylinder in early March 2026 and by a further ₹29 per cylinder in June, resulting in a cumulative increase of around 10.3 per cent. Kerosene and other fuel items also witnessed an increase in prices. Electricity prices, however, recorded a decline on a y-o-y basis on account of reduction in tariffs and provision of free or subsidised electricity in certain states (C hart IV.13a ). Within transport fuel, retail prices of petrol and diesel were increased in four successive rounds during the month of May leading to a 7.5 per cent increase for petrol and 8.4 per cent for diesel ( Chart IV.13b ). The magnitude of domestic price increases was however moderate as compared to the increase in global prices ( Chart IV.14 ). Part of the shock was absorbed by the Government by reducing the Special Additional Excise Duty on petrol and diesel by ₹10 per litre each in March to ease the burden on domestic consumers. After the initial surge, global oil prices have remained highly volatile with sharp two-way movements triggered by geopolitical developments. Amidst renewed uncertainty about the US-Iran negotiations, Indian basket crude oil prices increased from US$82 per barrel in July to around US$116 per barrel in September. 19 Tightness in refined product markets also continues with low diesel inventories, higher stock drawdowns and the crude futures curve in backwardation. 20 These conditions, along with elevated refined product margins, pose upside risks to domestic fuel

prices if geopolitical disruptions persist. Core CPI (CPI excluding Food and Fuel) Core inflation (CPI excluding food and fuel) 21 increased from 3.7 per cent in April to 4.2 per cent in August 2026. Core inflation excluding precious metals 22 registered a sharper increase from 2.2 per cent to 2.9 per cent during the same period ( Table IV.1 ). Precious metals, which are part of the ‘personal care and effects’ sub-group, were a major driver of core inflation over the last year. During April-December 2025, gold and silver prices rose by 41.6 per cent and 66.3 per cent, respectively, accounting for about one-third of the overall core inflation during this period. After peaking in January 2026, precious metal prices have remained range-bound. In terms of sub-components, housing, restaurants and accommodation services, and clothing and footwear were the other major contributors to core inflation ( Chart IV.15 ). Box IV.1: Measuring Inflation Generalisation through the Diffusion Index When confronted with supply shocks, monetary policy responses are calibrated based on the assessment of second-round effects. If supply shocks are temporary, monetary policy often looks through them, whereas when there are signs of generalisation, policy acts to prevent inflation from becoming embedded in expectations. One critical challenge in this context is to gauge the extent to which inflation has become generalised. This can be assessed by examining whether the initial price pressures remain confined to the directly affected components or have spread to a wider set of items in the CPI basket. A useful measure of this generalisation is the inflation diffusion index, which captures the weighted distribution of item-level price changes in the CPI basket (de Soyres et al., 2026). An increase in the diffusion index in the high inflation categories indicates that price pressures are becoming

more widespread across the consumption basket. This can be used along with the headline or core inflation numbers to understand the nature of inflation process. An increase in headline inflation accompanied by a low diffusion index for the high inflation categories is indicative of inflation driven by idiosyncratic supply shocks. On the other hand, surge in diffusion index in the higher inflation category along with the headline inflation number, indicates that inflationary pressures have become more broad-based and generalised. Many countries use diffusion indices alongside other measures of underlying inflation to understand the spread of inflationary pressures. 25 Over the years, the Reserve Bank of India has also examined the distribution of item-level inflation using diffusion indices, inflation distributions and kernel density plots (RBI, Monetary Policy Report, various issues; Nadhanael and Pattanaik, 2010; Hasan et al, 2026). Against this backdrop, the box attempts to compile diffusion indices for inflation in India based on the revised CPI (2024=100) series. The diffusion indices are compiled for i) Headline CPI comprising all items; and ii) Core or CPI excluding food and fuel. 26 The indices are constructed using weighted item-level year-on-year (y-o-y) inflation rates. 27 Conceptually, diffusion indices represent the weighted share of items in the respective CPI basket, categorised into the following four buckets (intervals), aligning it with the inflation target and its tolerance band: i. Below 2 per cent; ii. Between 2 per cent and 4 per cent; iii. Between 4 per cent and 6 per cent; and iv. Above 6 per cent. IV.4 Drivers of Inflation Trajectory This section analyses the evolution of inflation conditions based on the assessment of underlying factors. Imported Inflation The contribution of imported components to domestic inflation picked up in 2026 following the onset of the West Asia conflict. Imported inflation as per the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) (2022-23=100) registered a significant increase up to May 2026, with some pullback thereafter, driven by petroleum products ( Chart IV.20 ). CPI imported inflation also remained elevated during this period, mainly due to higher precious metals prices, given the larger relative weight of precious metals in CPI. 30 The extent of sequential increase in imported inflation in CPI since the onset of the West Asia conflict was lower than that in WPI, partly on account of delayed and partial price increases in petroleum products at the retail level. Cost Conditions Input cost pressures, as measured by WPI industrial raw materials and farm inputs inflation, rose sharply during March-May and remained elevated thereafter. The acceleration in industrial input costs was led by petroleum products, particularly aviation turbine fuel (ATF), high-speed diesel (HSD), naphtha, bitumen, furnace oil, and petroleum coke. The increase in farm input cost inflation was driven mainly by HSD, fertilisers, and nitrogen compounds ( Chart IV.21 ). In the organised corporate sector, staff cost growth (y-o-y) in manufacturing accelerated in Q1:2026-27, following a moderation in Q4:2025-26 driven by strong momentum. In the services sector, y-o-y staff cost growth moderated

during both Q4:2025-26 and Q1:2026-27, despite a positive momentum, on account of unfavourable base effects ( Chart IV.22 ). On the outlook for cost and price conditions, infrastructure and services firms expect both input cost and selling price pressures to abate during Q3:2026-27, as per the firms polled in the Reserve Bank’s enterprise surveys. Manufacturing firms expect a moderation in input cost pressures while also expecting an increase in selling prices. Salary outgo pressures are expected to increase for manufacturing firms during Q3:2026-27. In contrast, it is expected to ease for services and infrastructure firms ( Chart IV.23 ). The Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) surveys indicate some sequential moderation in manufacturing firms’ cost pressures after the sharp increase following the onset of the West Asia conflict. Input price pressures reported by manufacturing firms eased gradually up to August 2026 after peaking in April. Output price pressures followed a broadly similar trajectory. Both input and output prices inched up in September. The manufacturing PMI input-output price gap turned positive in March 2026, indicating weak pass-through of input costs to selling prices. Although the gap narrowed from its March peak, it remained positive in August, suggesting some pent-up pass-through ( Chart IV.24a ). In the services sector, operating cost pressures eased gradually up to July before a mild pick-up in August 2026. Selling price pressures also moderated up to June but increased in July-August. Consequently, the services PMI input-output price gap narrowed significantly in August ( Chart IV.24b ). Similar trends were observed for Output and Input Producer Price Index (PPI) 31 for manufactured products during April-August 2026. For most industry groups, pace of increase in input prices was faster than that of output prices, suggesting that the full extent of input price rise may not have been passed on to output

prices ( Chart IV.25 ). At the aggregate level, however, output prices rose faster than input prices driven by coke and refined petroleum products. Margins Food price margins 32 have recorded a mixed trend in the recent period. Retail margins for cereals remained stable during April-September 2026. Margins for pulses remained stable until June before moderating during July-September. For TOP vegetables, margins picked up since April. In case of edible oils, margins peaked in May 2026 but remained range-bound thereafter ( Chart IV.26 ). In terms of the relative contribution of supply and demand factors in conditioning inflation dynamics, the evidence points towards the dissipation of both favourable supply and benign demand conditions, which led to increase in inflation in 2026-27 so far ( Box IV.2 ). Box IV.2: What Drives Inflation in India? Disentangling Demand and Supply Factors Disentangling the relative roles of demand and supply factors in driving inflation is critical for an inflation-targeting central bank to calibrate appropriate policy response. Demand-driven inflation typically calls for monetary tightening, while supply-driven inflation creates difficult policy trade-offs as it is often accompanied by a slowdown in growth. In case of India, the recent experience of inflation significantly undershooting the target before a sharp reversal merits a thorough examination of the role of demand and supply factors in shaping the inflation dynamics. Empirical literature has adopted different approaches to disentangle the contributions of aggregate demand and supply conditions such as identifying the cyclical component of inflation by examining its relationship with economic activity as proposed by Stock and Watson (2020). Another approach is to explicitly decompose inflation into demand and supply-driven components using price and quantity information at the commodity or consumption-category level (Shapiro, 2024 33 and Shekhar, Kishore and Bhoi, 2023). More recently, Eickmeier and Hofmann (2025) have developed a

structural factor model to identify aggregate demand and supply conditions using a broad set of inflation and real activity indicators. Their methodology exploits the common variation across a large number of macroeconomic series and identifies demand and supply factors through theoretically motivated sign restrictions on factor loadings. The demand factor is characterised by positive co-movement between inflation and economic activity, whereas the supply factor is associated with opposite movements in inflation and economic activity. This framework enables the construction of aggregate indicators of demand and supply conditions and facilitates an assessment of their contribution to inflation dynamics over time. This factor-based approach is applied to the Indian economy to identify indicators of aggregate demand and supply conditions and examine their role in the evolution of inflation in India. Compared with approaches that focus primarily on cyclical inflation or commodity-level price and quantity responses, the proposed framework incorporates information from a broader set of macroeconomic variables. Data The dataset includes a broad set of inflation measures including headline CPI, house price index, and other group/sub-group-wise inflation. The real-activity block includes GDP and expenditure components, gross and sectoral GVA indices, and other demand proxies such as diesel consumption and capacity utilisation. Other global price indicators like gold, copper, Brent crude oil and fertiliser prices are also included. 34 Methodology The empirical strategy uses a factor model estimated by employing principal component analysis on quarterly macroeconomic time series data for India. Factor identification follows the standard supply-demand analysis based on randomly generated orthogonal rotations. The demand factor is identified as one that loads positively on inflation measures and real-activity measures. The supply factor is identified as one that loads negatively on inflation measures and positively on real-activity measures. Sign restrictions are imposed across key variables while allowing some variables to remain unrestricted. Once

the demand and supply factors are identified 35 , Fry-Pagan median target approach is used to select accepted rotation closest to the median target. Results The findings indicate that the recent episode of inflation declining from H2:2024-25 to H2:2025-26 was driven by a weakening of demand as well as easy supply conditions ( Chart IV.2.1 and Chart IV.2.2 ). Latest data for Q1:2026-27 show closing of negative demand conditions as well as waning of easy supply conditions. Demand factor converged to almost zero levels during Q1 as economic activity strengthened despite global shocks and emerging supply side pressures. As growth has surprised on the upside and inflation is showing early signs of generalisation, this indicates waning of favourable factors that kept inflation benign during 2025-26 and potential pressures going forward. IV.5 Conclusion Headline inflation has increased steadily throughout 2026-27 (up to August), initially driven by higher food and fuel inflation but showing signs of broad-based price pressures in recent months. The impact of El Niño conditions and deficient southwest monsoon is increasingly reflected in

food prices. Core inflation recorded a pick-up along with incipient signs of generalisation. Going forward, there is a material risk that supply-side pressures in food may remain unabated as weather uncertainties persist and global oil prices continue to remain volatile. In this context, generalisation of inflation through second-round effects remains a major risk from the firming up of demand conditions, given strong growth impulses. Macroeconomic Outlook Amidst persistent geopolitical tensions, volatility in global commodity and financial markets and persisting trade uncertainty, India’s economic activity remains robust, supported

by resilient domestic demand, strengthening investment and sound macroeconomic fundamentals. Headline inflation has firmed up in recent months, largely reflecting food and fuel price pressures, but with increasing evidence of generalisation. The outlook for growth and inflation is subject to uncertainties arising from external economic environment, commodity prices, weather events and global financial conditions. Against this backdrop, monetary policy remains focussed on maintaining price stability while supporting sustained economic growth. V.1 Key Developments since the April 2026 MPR Since the release of the Monetary Policy Report (MPR) in April 2026, the global economy has continued to navigate an uncertain environment precipitated by geopolitical tensions, evolving trade and tariff stipulations, volatile financial conditions, and rapid technological change. Despite these headwinds, global economic activity has remained resilient, with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projecting global growth at 3.0 per cent in 2026 and 3.4 per cent in 2027. 1 The inflation outlook, however, is of material concern with global headline inflation projected to rise from 4.1 per cent in 2025 to 4.7 per cent in 2026 by the IMF, suggesting that the disinflation process that was underway since early 2024 has reversed its course. Macroeconomic dynamics have been multi-paced across countries, reflecting the varying level of exposure to geopolitical developments, state of domestic demand conditions and extent of involvement in the ongoing technology-related investment cycle. Against this backdrop, monetary policy has been cautious in major economies with central banks balancing the risk of renewed inflationary pressures against concerns on slowing economic activity. Financial markets, meanwhile, have remained resilient, albeit with intermittent bouts of volatility in the wake of the prevailing uncertainty. Global equity markets have generally been supported by strong corporate earnings and optimism around technology-related investment, even as geopolitical uncertainties and macroeconomic data releases led to periodic corrections. Sovereign bond yields,

particularly at longer maturities, have hardened across major economies amidst concerns over inflation, elevated public debt and large financing requirements. Global commodity prices have been volatile since April 2026, with the West Asia conflict induced initial surge moderating across some segments before renewed supply concerns triggered price pressures again since August. Energy markets were particularly sensitive to supply disruptions. Similarly, metal prices remained elevated amidst supply disruptions, supported by strong demand from infrastructure and technology-related investment, before moderating subsequently and rising again since August. The emergence of El Niño conditions has also added uncertainty to the outlook for agricultural production and food prices. Agricultural commodity prices, which were relatively stable after April, faced upward pressures from higher energy and fertiliser costs, adverse weather conditions and disruptions to trade and supplies. These developments were also reflected in currency markets with varying level of exchange rate adjustments across major economies. Fluctuations in the US dollar and evolving monetary policy expectations contributed to changing currency dynamics, while higher energy prices continued to exert pressure on some energy-importing economies. Amidst this volatile backdrop, the global economy has so far demonstrated resilience, although the interplay of geopolitical developments, inflationary pressures and financial market conditions will remain the key in shaping the outlook ahead. On the domestic front, economic activity remained robust in Q1:2026–27, with real GDP expanding by 7.8 per cent and real GVA by 8.2 per cent. Growth remains broad-based, with strong momentum in industry and services, while agriculture and allied activities also contributed positively. On the expenditure side, private consumption remained resilient and investment activity strengthened, with gross fixed capital formation registering a notable expansion. Headline CPI inflation increased from 3.5 per cent in April 2026 to 4.8 per cent in August, driven by sustained positive price momentum. Food inflation firmed up during

this period and contributed significantly to the increase in headline inflation. Fuel inflation, which had remained subdued earlier, started increasing from May due to elevated international energy prices and their pass-through to domestic prices, albeit partially. Core inflation recorded only a modest increase till July before accelerating in August amidst signs of generalisation. Against this growth-inflation dynamics, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) considered it prudent to wait for the implications of prevailing uncertainties on growth and greater clarity on the inflation outlook to emerge before undertaking any policy action. Therefore, following the cumulative easing of 125 basis points during February to December 2025, the MPC left the policy repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent in its April, June and August 2026 meetings while retaining the neutral stance. Monetary Policy Committee Meetings: April 2026-September 2026 The MPC met for its first policy of the financial year in April 2026, amidst heightened geopolitical tensions arising from the West Asia conflict, which severely disrupted global supply chains, posing headwinds for India. The Indian economy, however, remained resilient, though elevated energy and commodity prices and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz were expected to weigh adversely on domestic economic activity and inflation in 2026-27. Considering all these factors, real GDP growth for 2026-27 was projected at 6.9 per cent with downside risks while CPI headline inflation was projected at 4.6 per cent with upside risks. Core inflation was projected at 4.4 per cent for 2026-27. Recognising the supply-side nature of the shock and strong fundamentals of the domestic economy, the MPC considered it prudent to wait and unanimously decided to keep the repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent while retaining the neutral stance. At the June 2026 meeting, the continuing West Asia conflict posed risks to inflation and growth; nonetheless, domestic economic

activity remained broadly resilient. Elevated energy and commodity prices and persistent supply disruptions were expected to weigh on growth. Consequently, real GDP growth projection for 2026-27 was revised downwards by 30 basis points (bps) to 6.6 per cent. Meanwhile, marginal pick up in headline CPI inflation in March and April, primarily due to higher food inflation and subsequent increases in retail fuel prices, raised inflationary pressures, leading to an upward revision of the CPI inflation projection for 2026-27 to 5.1 per cent. Core inflation was projected at 4.7 per cent for 2026-27. The MPC noted that while the risks to inflation have increased, it would be prudent to await for greater clarity on the evolving outlook. Accordingly, the MPC unanimously decided to retain the policy repo rate at 5.25 per cent along with the neutral stance. In the run up to the August 2026 meeting, the global economic outlook remained volatile as the relief from temporary ceasefire dissipated quickly. Domestically, risks to agriculture emanated from an erratic monsoon and El Niño conditions and supply-side measures were undertaken to mitigate the impact. Overall, the Indian economy demonstrated resilience, driven by better-than-expected consumption and investment demand, despite persistent global headwinds. Accordingly, real GDP growth projection for 2026-27 was revised slightly upwards to 6.7 per cent. On the inflation front, CPI inflation rose to 4.4 per cent in June 2026 after remaining below the target of 4.0 per cent for 16 consecutive months, but was 30 bps lower than projections, prompting a downward revision of the 2026-27 inflation projection to 5.0 per cent. The core inflation was also projected lower at 4.3 per cent for 2026-27. The MPC observed that the rise in headline inflation was mainly driven by supply-side pressures and considered it appropriate for greater clarity to emerge on the inflation

outlook before taking policy action. Accordingly, the MPC unanimously voted to keep the policy repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent and retained the neutral stance. Nevertheless, the MPC pointed out that any policy action would also consider the recalibration of policy rates in line with the evolving growth-inflation dynamics, especially normalisation of the underlying inflation from its earlier benign levels. The Indian MPC’s unanimous voting pattern stands in contrast to the diversity in voting witnessed in many other central banks ( Table V.1 ). Monetary policy decisions remained divergent across economies based on domestic conditions, although a tilt towards hawkish pivot is visible. Among the Advanced Economies (AEs), while policy rate remained broadly unchanged, dissent among the members was more pronounced. Japan and the UK witnessed voting disagreements in all their meetings, while the US saw dissent in two out of four meetings with a rate hike in its latest meeting. Among the Emerging Market Economies (EMEs), pivot towards hiking is visible for some although Brazil and Hungary have reduced their policy rates by 100 bps and 75 bps, respectively, in view of high real policy rates. Factors conditioning the Macroeconomic Outlook Macroeconomic developments pertaining to economic activity and inflation during H1:2026-27 are analysed in chapters III and IV. Going forward, the outlook is based on a set of baseline assumptions. First, assumption on crude oil price has been revised up to US$95 per barrel for the second half of 2026-27 from US$85 per barrel for 2026-27 in the last MPR ( Table V.2 ). This makes the alternate scenario presented in MPR April 2026 as our baseline with a $10 per barrel rise in oil price assumption over 2026- 27 and 2027-28. International crude oil prices peaked in April 2026 primarily because of severe supply shock caused by the West Asia conflict. Following the signing of Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran in June, oil prices eased and reached around US$83 per barrel in July 2026. After the ceasefire violations and the consequent collapse of the US-Iran agreement, prices began to firm up in August and further escalated in September. The Brent futures curve, however, remained in backwardation, with expectations of prices easing in future ( Chart V.1a ). The upward pressure on prices was mitigated to some extent due to destocking of crude oil inventory by several countries, which has witnessed sharp depletion since Q4:2025-26, with minimal support to prices expected in the months ahead. With steady increase in production, crude oil inventory is expected to be replenished in the second half of 2026-27 that might keep demand and price pressures high ( Chart V.1b ). Second, the nominal exchange rate of the Indian rupee (₹) remained in the range of ₹92–97 per US dollar during April–September 2026 ( Chart V.1c ). The rupee depreciated towards the end of April driven by portfolio outflows that reflected a risk off sentiment towards EMEs under heightened uncertainty. Subsequently, the rupee reversed its trend, supported by the easing of geopolitical tensions and the announcement of measures by the Reserve Bank of India to attract foreign capital flows including USD-INR swap window for FCNR(B) deposits and foreign investment in government securities. The Indian rupee subsequently weakened in early July in tandem with rising crude oil prices, but

has since remained range-bound. Considering the volatility of the US dollar and fluctuations in global capital flows, the baseline assumption for the exchange rate has been revised to ₹95 per US dollar as against ₹94 in the April 2026 MPR. Third, according to the IMF, global economic growth is projected at 3.0 per cent in 2026 and 3.4 per cent in 2027, lower than 3.5 per cent registered during 2025 ( Chart V.2 ). The prolonged conflict in West Asia continues to pose significant downside risk, with the potential to exacerbate supply-chain disruptions, and tighten financial conditions. AEs are projected to grow at 1.7 per cent in 2026, marginally lower than 1.9 per cent in 2025, while growth in EMEs is expected to decline to 3.8 per cent in 2026 from 4.5 per cent in 2025. In its Economic Outlook (September 2026), the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) projected global GDP at 2.9 per cent in 2026 and 3.0 per cent in 2027. According to the IMF, world trade volume is expected to moderate sharply from 5.0 per cent in 2025 to 3.5 per cent in 2026 before recovering to 4.3 per cent in 2027. This moderation reflects the easing of earlier front-loading, tariff-related headwinds and the gradual reconfiguration of trade and production networks, partly offset by robust growth in technology-related trade flows. Global inflation is projected to reverse its declining trajectory temporarily, rising from 4.1 per cent in 2025 to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 3.9 per cent in 2027, primarily reflecting higher energy and food prices in 2026. V.2 Inflation Outlook Domestic headline inflation edged up to 4.8 per cent in August, driven primarily by rising food and fuel prices but with increasing evidence of broad-basing of price pressures as evident from diffusion

indices (as discussed in Chapter IV). Inflation in food and beverages rose to 5.7 per cent, while core inflation inched up to 4.2 per cent. Going forward, inflation trajectory remains subject to considerable upside risks from overlapping climate and geopolitical shocks. Domestically, outlook is clouded by recent projections from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), USA, warning that the prevailing El Niño phenomenon is set to intensify till the end of 2026 and remain strong in the first half of 2027, posing downside risks to agriculture output, and reservoir replenishment. On the external front, developments in West Asia pose key upside risks, particularly through their impact on global energy prices, commodity markets and supply chains. Renewed geopolitical tensions have kept energy markets volatile and could raise freight, insurance and other transportation costs. Any sustained increase in these costs could feed into domestic retail prices and raise input costs across a range of products, triggering the risk of second-round and broader cost-push pressures. Urban households’ inflation expectations for the next three months as well as one year ahead rose by 70 bps and 60 bps to 9.9 per cent and 10.0 per cent, respectively, in the latest survey round (September 2026) of the Reserve Bank’s bi-monthly households survey. 2 The proportion of respondents anticipating a rise in general inflation has inched up for both the time horizons ( Chart V.3a ). Additionally, according to the Reserve Bank’s recent bi-monthly Rural Consumer Confidence Survey (RCCS) 3 , the current perception (vis-à-vis a year ago) of inflation in rural and semi-urban households increased by 70 bps to 6.8 per cent in September 2026 as compared with the previous round. Moreover, their one-year ahead expectations also rose by 50 bps to 7.9 per cent. A sequential rise in the inflation expectations has been

observed since January 2026 survey round as against the declining trend during the calendar year 2025 (Chart V.3b). Manufacturing firms surveyed in the July-September 2026 round of the Reserve Bank’s quarterly Industrial Outlook Survey expect pressures from cost of raw materials to persist in Q3:2026-27 with increased pass-through to selling prices ( Chart V.4a ). 4 Services and infrastructure sectors expect some easing of input cost pressures in Q3:2026-27, resulting in moderation in the pace of increase of selling prices ( Chart V.4b and V.4c ). 5 Professional forecasters surveyed by the Reserve Bank in September 2026 projected CPI inflation to increase from 3.9 per cent in Q1:2026-27 to 4.9 per cent in Q2. It is expected to increase further to 5.9 per cent in Q3:2026-27, then moderate to 5.5 per cent in Q4 and further to 4.7 per cent in Q2:2027-28 ( Chart V.5a and Table V.3 ). 6 CPI inflation, excluding food and fuel 7 , is expected at 4.1 per cent during Q2:2026-27, and thereafter remain between 4.3 to 4.7 per cent till Q2:2027-28. Long-run inflation expectations of professional forecasters – measured by their five- and ten-year horizons – is at 4.5 per cent and 4.2 per cent, respectively, in the current round ( Chart V.5 b ). Considering the initial conditions, signals from forward-looking surveys and estimates from time-series and structural models 8 , CPI inflation is projected to average 5.2 per cent in 2026-27 with Q2 at 4.9 per cent; Q3 at 6.0 per cent; and Q4 at 5.7 per cent with risks evenly balanced ( Chart V.6 and Table V.3 ). Assuming a normal monsoon, and no further exogenous or policy shocks, structural model estimates indicate that inflation will average 5.0 per cent in 2027-28. The 50 per cent and the 70 per cent

confidence intervals for headline inflation in Q4:2027-28 are 3.1-6.1 per cent and 2.3-6.9 per cent, respectively. V.3 Growth Outlook Domestic economic activity remains resilient supported by private consumption and fixed investment. High-capacity utilisation, robust bank credit growth, conducive financial conditions, and the government’s continued emphasis on infrastructure are expected to stimulate investment activity. Moreover, several measures announced in the Union Budget 2026-27 are also growth supportive. However,

spillovers from heightened geopolitical tensions, along with volatility in international financial markets and trade dynamics, pose downside risks to the growth outlook. Forward-looking surveys offer additional insights. The bi-monthly consumer confidence (current situation index) for urban households remained almost at a similar level in September 2026 vis-à-vis the previous round. Consumer confidence of rural households registered a decline in the latest survey round, dipping further into pessimistic zone ( Chart V.7 ). Consumers’ optimism for the year ahead, measured by the future expectations index, remained in positive territory; however, it continued to decline for both urban and rural households in the recent survey round, driven mainly by lower expectations across most survey parameters ( Chart V.7 ). In the Reserve Bank’s quarterly industrial outlook survey of July-September 2026, manufacturing firms continued to stay optimistic and recorded improved sentiments of the firms from the previous quarter about the business conditions (BAI/BEI) 9 ( Chart V.8a ). The services firms experienced some moderation in sentiments in Q3:2026-27 as compared to previous quarter, while optimism increased for infrastructure firms ( Charts V.8b and V.8c ). Professional forecasters polled in the September 2026 round of the Reserve Bank’s survey expect real GDP growth to be at 7.2 per cent during Q2:2026-27. Growth is expected at about 6.8-7.1 per cent during the subsequent four quarters ( Chart V.9 ). Taking into account the baseline assumptions, survey indicators and model forecasts, real GDP growth is expected at 7.1 per cent in 2026-27 with 7.2 per cent in Q2; 6.9 per cent in Q3 and 6.8 per cent in Q4 – with risks evenly balanced around this baseline path ( Chart V.10 and Table V.3 ). Assuming a normal monsoon and no major exogenous or policy shocks, structural model estimates for 2027-28 place real GDP growth at

7.0 per cent. There are upside and downside risks to the baseline growth estimate. Upside risks emanate from easing of geopolitical tensions, abating of trade-related uncertainty and a broad-based revival in private investment. On the downside, spillovers from prolonged geopolitical tensions, volatility in global financial markets, shifting trade patterns, and climate-related shocks pose risks to the baseline growth path. V.4 Balance of Risks The baseline projections of domestic growth and inflation remain conditional on key domestic and global macroeconomic assumptions that are given in Table V.2 . These assumptions are subject to evolving uncertainties from ongoing geopolitical tensions in West Asia, commodity price volatility, global trade fragmentation, and domestic weather-related risks. Against this backdrop, this section outlines the balance of risks surrounding the baseline projections under plausible alternative scenarios. (i) Global Growth Uncertainties Global economic activity is navigating crosscurrents from ongoing war-induced supply shocks and a positive technology-led investment cycle. Growth momentum remains highly uneven, with advanced and emerging economies that are integrated into the artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor value chains experiencing technology-driven growth. In contrast, activity across energy-importing and non-tech economies are constrained by elevated energy prices, structural headwinds, and trade disruptions. Downside risks to global growth dominate. Broadening geopolitical conflicts in the West Asia may continue to disrupt global supply chains and critical maritime transit routes, particularly the Strait of Hormuz. This continued escalation of geopolitical hostilities may further disrupt the commodity markets. Moreover, elevated policy uncertainty and a potential surge in trade protectionism may restrain international trade flows and investment. High public debt levels in major economies leave sovereign markets exposed to financial tightening, restricting the fiscal space for productive investment. Downside risk also originate from potential sharp downside corrections in AI-related asset valuations which pose contagion risks to global financial markets. On the upside, a

durable resolution of geopolitical tensions, swifter normalisation in energy markets, and faster AI-driven productivity gains could lift global growth above the baseline. If global growth turns out to be 100 bps below the baseline, domestic growth and inflation could be lower by around 30 bps and 15 bps, respectively. Conversely, if global growth is higher by 50 bps relative to the baseline, domestic growth and inflation could turn out to be higher by around 15 bps and 7 bps, respectively ( Charts V.11a and V.12a ). (ii) International Crude Oil Prices Global crude oil markets remain volatile due to supply disruptions in the Gulf region. After prices surged following the onset of the West Asia conflict, brent crude oil scaled a peak of US$105 per barrel in late July 2026 following renewed hostilities and maritime disruptions, before easing to around US$90 per barrel by end August 2026. Prices rose to an average of US$114 during September 2026. According to the Oil Market Report by International Energy Agency (IEA), approximately 10.0 million barrels per day (mb/d) of Gulf output remained unavailable as of August 2026. The IEA projects global oil supply to contract by 5.7 mb/d, while global oil demand is expected to decline by 2.5 mb/d in 2026. The primary upside risks originate from significant supply disruption due to prolonged West Asia conflict, which could threaten major energy infrastructure or further restrict critical maritime transit routes. Additionally, deeper, or prolonged production constraints by major oil-exporting nations, combined with depleted global inventory buffers, could severely tighten supply. If these shocks materialise, a sustained spike in crude oil prices would rapidly transmit to domestic inflation through higher imported fuel costs and second round effects ( Box V.1 ). Assuming full pass-through to domestic product prices, if crude oil prices are higher by

10 per cent than the baseline, inflation could turn out to be higher by around 50 bps and growth may be lower by around 15 bps. Conversely, sharper-than-expected deceleration in global growth, an accelerated resolution to ongoing geopolitical hostilities or robust production increases from non-traditional suppliers could ease prices. If crude oil prices are lower by 10 per cent relative to the baseline, inflation could be lower by around 50 bps and GDP growth could be higher by 15 bps ( Charts V.11a and V.12a ). Box V.1: Crude Oil Price Shocks: Quantifying the Macroeconomic Impact on the Indian Economy Being an energy importer, crude oil price dynamics remain a critical determinant of macroeconomic stability in India, exerting a profound influence on domestic price stability, external sector balances, and overall growth outlook. Global crude oil prices have experienced extreme volatility in 2026 so far, driven by the West Asian conflict and supply chain disruptions. The Indian crude oil basket spiked to around US$125 per barrel in March 2026. Prices subsequently eased to an average of US$82 per barrel in July, before rising to US$90 per barrel by August 2026. The renewed West Asia conflict has pushed up crude oil prices to $116 per barrel in September 2026. Given India’s heavy reliance on external energy sources, adverse international crude price shocks pose significant pass-through risks to headline inflation – both directly through fuel components and indirectly via generalised cost-push pressures, creating headwinds to medium-term macroeconomic stability. Furthermore, the broader global energy outlook remains clouded by several compounding factors including widespread uncertainty regarding the timeline for supply resumption and the restoration of critical shipping routes. Additionally, global strategic petroleum reserves remain low, leaving markets vulnerable to further shocks. To evaluate how these price fluctuations ripple through the economy, the Quarterly Projection Model

(QPM) is utilised to delineate several interconnected channels through which the increase in crude oil prices impacts the economy (John et.al., 2022, 2023). An escalation in crude oil prices adversely impacts key global macroeconomic aggregates, aggravating global inflationary pressures, dampening output growth, possibly triggering higher monetary policy rates. Heightened global energy prices cause import bill to rise, putting downward pressure on the domestic currency, leading to rise in imported inflation. An immediate pass-through of international price movements to domestic energy prices exert an instantaneous upward pressure on headline inflation, capturing the direct effect. The increase in petroleum product prices triggers indirect cost push effects emanating from firms passing on higher input costs, pushing up prices of final goods and services. Concurrently, elevated energy prices compress household real disposable incomes and narrow corporate profit margins, precipitating a contraction in discretionary consumer spending and private investment. This resultant moderation in aggregate demand has a dampening effect on inflationary pressures. To prevent inflation expectations from getting unhinged, the central bank could raise policy rates. This monetary tightening widens the output gap and compresses demand to bring inflation back to target. Chart V.1.1 depicts the decomposition of impact on headline inflation due to a persistent 10 per cent shock in crude oil prices highlighting the relative strength of the channels of transmission. Higher inflation in the first year is primarily driven by the direct effects, which dissipates over the next year. In the medium term, indirect cost push effects play the prominent role. While the demand channel exerts a moderating impact on price pressures, its offsetting impact is considerably smaller than that of the cost-push channel. Furthermore, monetary policy reaction also imparts a consequential dampening effect on inflation in the medium-term. In the case of output growth, the favourable impact of exchange rate depreciation

will only be evident in the first year but this impact will be more than offset by moderation in domestic demand as well as weaker global growth. The pass-through of a depreciated currency turns contractionary in the subsequent year, as higher imported costs exert pressure on macroeconomic output ( Chart V.1.2 ). (iii) Exchange Rate The Indian Rupee (INR) was supported by robust FCNR(B) deposit inflows in early September 2026, subsequently, these gains were reversed due to higher crude oil prices. Looking ahead, the INR may face headwinds, including a robust US dollar, elevated import cost, volatile capital inflows and rise in trade policy uncertainties. Any escalation in geopolitical tensions or unexpectedly aggressive monetary tightening by major central banks may put pressure on INR. Conversely, the INR could find support from the resilience of India’s services exports, the stability in bilateral trade frameworks and sustained foreign capital inflows. In a scenario where the INR depreciates by 5 per cent over the baseline, inflation could be higher by around 40 bps, while GDP growth may benefit by around 25 bps through the exports channel in the short term, under normal macroeconomic conditions. In contrast, an appreciation of the INR by 5 per cent relative to the baseline would moderate both inflation and GDP growth by around 40 bps and 25 bps, respectively ( Charts V.11b and V.12b ). (iv) Food Inflation Domestic headline CPI inflation experienced an uptick in mid-2026, driven primarily by food price pressures. Price pressures across

all the classes within the food and beverage basket firmed up. Risk to agricultural crops remain in the wake of deficient and erratic monsoon experienced in 2026-27. Food price risks remain sensitive to weather variations. Adverse impact of El Niño, unseasonal rain, lower reservoir levels, localised heatwaves, higher input costs pose upside risks to food inflation, which may result in headline inflation being higher by 40 bps vis-à-vis the baseline. On the other hand, large buffer stocks, and government's various supply side measures could moderate headline inflation by around 40 bps relative to the baseline ( Charts V.11b and V.12b ). V.5 Conclusion India’s macroeconomic outlook continues to be supported by resilient domestic economic activity on the back of private consumption and investment. The external environment, however, remains uncertain. At the same time, improving investment outlook, bilateral trade agreements and conducive financial conditions could provide further support to economic activity. On the inflation front, the recent increase in headline inflation has been driven largely by food and fuel prices, but core inflation has also registered a pickup from its benign levels, indicating signs of greater generalisation of price pressures as evident from diffusion indices. Going forward, upside risks to the inflation outlook persist from renewed geopolitical tensions, disruptions to energy supplies and adverse weather conditions. Against this backdrop, potential second-round effects warrant stricter vigilance particularly as demand conditions remain strong. Overall, the outlook for growth and inflation will depend on how domestic demand and supply conditions evolve alongside developments in the global economy, with the balance of risks remaining contingent on these factors. _________________________________________________________________________________ 1 World Economic Outlook (WEO) Update, International Monetary Fund (IMF), July 2026. 2 The Reserve Bank’s inflation expectations survey of households is being conducted in 19 cities since March 2021 (18 cities in the previous rounds)
